mem.t: Come to me, all you who labour and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.

lessons.title: God Pressed Pause
lessons.theme: God rested on the seventh day; rest is his own design

v: On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done.
God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy, because he rested in it from all his work of creation which he had done.
You shall labour six days, and do all your work,

but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates;
for in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day, and made it holy.

lessons.still: Before work, rest your hands on your knees and stop all movement for thirty seconds. Say to the Lord: “Lord, when you finished your work, you rested. I will work hard today, but I am not what holds the world up. You are.”
teach: When creation was complete, Scripture records a surprising act: “On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work” (Gen. 2:2). Almighty God does not grow tired. He rested not from weakness but to establish a rhythm. Later, at Sinai, that rhythm was written into the Ten Commandments: “You shall labour six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God” (Exod. 20:9–10). Sons and daughters, servants, livestock and the stranger within the gates were all included. Rest is not a privilege for the wealthy; it is God’s gift to every creature.

Company servers have a scheduled maintenance window: service paused, caches cleared, systems updated. No one calls that downtime a waste, because without it the system will eventually crash. People are no different. We assume that stopping means falling behind, when in fact refusing to stop is what really breaks us. God wrote rest into the weekly schedule as if he had booked you a standing maintenance window. Skip it, and you can keep going for a while, but not for a lifetime.

Refusing to stop often hides self-centredness: without me, everything will collapse; if I rest, others will overtake me. The Sabbath trains us in humility, letting people be people and letting God be God. Every time we stop work, we declare that the world is held up by God, not by me. Rest is not the prize for finishing our work; it is a lesson in faith. We are accepted first, and then we go to work.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus is my example and Scripture is my standard. Humility means laying down power and returning to my place. The Sabbath is exactly the day I lay down “I must control everything”, and confess that God is the one who holds all things together.
lessons.scene: Daniel runs a small interior design studio in Auckland and has hardly taken a full day off in four years. This Sunday morning his wife suggests a family trip to the beach, but he opens his laptop and says, “I’ll just answer a few client emails.” His little daughter stands in the doorway holding her bucket and spade.
q: Who is God? — Almighty God “rested from all his work”. What does that show you about his heart?
Who am I? — Is there a voice in you that says, “If I stop, everything will fall apart”? Where does it come from?
How shall I respond? — If you were Daniel, what would you choose this morning?
lessons.jesus: On the cross Jesus cried, “It is finished!” Then, on the Sabbath, he lay quietly in the tomb. The great work of redemption was complete, and he too “rested”. Our rest is built on the work he has already finished; we no longer need to earn God’s acceptance by our own toil.
lessons.pray: Lord, Creator of heaven and earth, thank you for showing me how to rest. I confess I often cannot stop, as though everything would spin out of control without me. Today I give you my work and my anxiety. Teach me to truly stop for one day this week and be renewed in your presence. Be King over my time. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Circle this week’s Sabbath in my calendar
List three work tasks I will not do on that day
Tell my family or flatmates my Sabbath plan
lessons.noon: “he rested in it from all his work of creation” — Lord, right now I rest awhile in you too.

lessons.title: Rules Made for People
lessons.theme: The Sabbath is a gift, not another appraisal form

v: He was going on the Sabbath day through the grain fields; and his disciples began, as they went, to pluck the ears of grain.
The Pharisees said to him, “Behold, why do they do that which is not lawful on the Sabbath day?”
He said to them, “Did you never read what David did when he had need and was hungry—he, and those who were with him?
How he entered into God’s house at the time of Abiathar the high priest, and ate the show bread, which is not lawful to eat except for the priests, and gave also to those who were with him?”
He said to them, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.
Therefore the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.”

lessons.still: Before work, drop your shoulders and take a deep breath. Say to the Lord: “Lord, you made rest for my good. Take away the chains in my heart today, and let me work lightly in you.”
teach: The disciples were walking through the grain fields, hungry, and plucked some ears of grain. The Pharisees pounced on the violation: “Behold, why do they do that which is not lawful on the Sabbath day?” (Mark 2:24). Jesus reminded them how David, when hungry, ate the show bread. Then he said something that overturns our thinking: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Therefore the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27–28). The Pharisees had turned the Sabbath into a dense rulebook; Jesus restored it as a gift of God’s love.

A hard hat on a building site is designed to protect the head; nobody trims their head to fit the hat. Yet we often turn good things into burdens. Rest becomes another appraisal form: did I keep it properly this week? Time with God becomes anxious counting of how many spiritual things I have done. The other extreme treats the Sabbath as a catch-up day for work. Both forget that this hard hat was made to measure for you by God himself.

The key is the final line: “the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.” At the centre of rest is not a rule but a person: Jesus. When he is King, the Sabbath becomes grace; when I am king, it becomes either law or an excuse. The question is not “Am I allowed to do this on the Sabbath?” but “On this day, am I letting Jesus have more of me?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus be King. Not the rulebook, not the workload, but the Lord of the Sabbath. A changed mindset changes how we live: from “I must keep the rules” to “I am invited by the Lord to rest”.
lessons.scene: Minghui is a ward sister at a hospital in Johor Bahru. She always rosters herself for weekend shifts so the young nurses can go home. This month she has missed church three Sundays in a row. When her small-group leader asks after her, her heart sinks; she wonders whether she is “not spiritual enough”. A colleague comes to ask if she can cover another shift.
q: Who is God? — Jesus is “lord even of the Sabbath”. With what heart did he give us rest?
Who am I? — Are you more likely to treat the Sabbath as an appraisal form, or as a catch-up day?
How shall I respond? — How can Minghui, working shifts, find a rhythm of rest that is truly hers?
lessons.jesus: On a Sabbath Jesus healed a man with a withered hand, knowing full well that the Pharisees were waiting to accuse him. He would rather be misunderstood than leave a man unhealed. In him, the Sabbath is no longer a cold regulation but a day when life is restored and people are seen.
lessons.pray: Lord of the Sabbath, thank you that you made rest for my good. Free me from two kinds of chains: turning rest into an appraisal, and spending rest on overtime. Today, as I look at rosters and calendars, help me keep space for you and for the people I love. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down one thing that truly gives me rest
If I work shifts, choose this week’s “alternative Sabbath”
Ask a colleague: have you had any rest lately?
lessons.noon: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.” — Lord, right now I receive the rest you give.

lessons.title: Manna Can’t Be Hoarded
lessons.theme: Receive each day’s provision daily; rest is trust in practice

v: This is the thing which the LORD has commanded: ‘Gather of it everyone according to his eating; an omer a head, according to the number of your persons, you shall take it, every man for those who are in his tent.’”
The children of Israel did so, and some gathered more, some less.
When they measured it with an omer, he who gathered much had nothing over, and he who gathered little had no lack. They each gathered according to his eating.
Moses said to them, “Let no one leave of it until the morning.”
Notwithstanding they didn’t listen to Moses, but some of them left of it until the morning, so it bred worms and became foul; and Moses was angry with them.
They gathered it morning by morning, everyone according to his eating. When the sun grew hot, it melted.

lessons.still: Before work, turn your palms upwards as if receiving. Say to the Lord: “Lord, give me today the strength, wisdom and patience I need for today. I will not hoard; I will trust you.”
teach: In the wilderness, manna lay on the ground every morning. God’s instruction was to gather according to each person’s eating, and Moses said, “Let no one leave of it until the morning” (Exod. 16:19). Some did not trust him and kept a little back, and “it bred worms and became foul” (Exod. 16:20). Wonderfully, “he who gathered much had nothing over, and he who gathered little had no lack” (Exod. 16:18). On the sixth day God gave a double portion, so that on the seventh they could stay home in peace. The Sabbath and the manna belong together: rest rests on trusting that God will provide again tomorrow.

Anyone who has worked in a fresh-food supermarket knows that fresh produce cannot be stockpiled; keep it too long and it has to be written off. Yet we are expert at hoarding security: one more contract just in case, one more late night so I am not outdone, one more savings goal first. Then the body is the first thing written off. Behind the hoarding lies a question: do I believe God will provide tomorrow? Manna does not teach laziness. It teaches us to gather diligently every day, and every day to entrust tomorrow to God.

The self-centred heart wants to control its own supply, as though gripping tighter means being safer; the self-emptied life learns to open its hands and receive daily. This does not rule out planning or saving; Scripture also teaches diligence and preparation. But when planning becomes fear-driven hoarding, it is a way of saying, “I don’t trust you.” Those who can stop today with a quiet heart are those who are sure that their provider is God, not their working hours.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Shift perspective from the human to the divine. Human logic says more is safer; God’s logic says trust is safer. Focus on Jesus, not your circumstances: tomorrow’s provision is in his hands, so today I can be at peace.
lessons.scene: Xinhong is a freelance video editor in Taipei. The year the pandemic hit, the work dried up, and since then he has said yes to everyone. He now has seven projects running at once and every weekend is booked. Another client messages: “Could you rush one more video this weekend? We’ll pay extra.”
q: Who is God? — God sent manna every day and was never late. What kind of provider does that show him to be?
Who am I? — What “security” do you hoard: work, savings, or other people’s approval?
How shall I respond? — How should Xinhong reply to this client in a way that springs from trust rather than fear?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I am the bread of life.” He taught his disciples to pray, “Give us today our daily bread” — not a year’s supply, but today’s. He himself depended on the Father day by day, and he invites us to come to him daily to receive, rather than stocking up once and walking away.
lessons.pray: Lord who provides day by day, thank you that I have never truly lacked. I confess that fear of tomorrow often makes me grab more, take on more and do more, squeezing my body and my family. Give me faith to do my part diligently today, and courage to say no, leaving room for rest. I believe you will be faithful tomorrow too. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Name one piece of work I took on out of fear
Practise declining one request beyond my capacity
Before bed, thank God for three specific provisions today
lessons.noon: “he who gathered much had nothing over, and he who gathered little had no lack” — Lord, right now I trust that today’s provision is just enough.

lessons.title: Change Yokes
lessons.theme: Come to Jesus; his yoke is easy and his burden light

v: “Come to me, all you who labour and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

lessons.still: Before work, lift your shoulders up towards your ears for three seconds, then slowly let them fall. Say to the Lord: “Lord, I give you every burden on my shoulders today. I will take your yoke and learn from you.”
teach: Jesus gives a gentle invitation: “Come to me, all you who labour and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matt. 11:28). Then he does not say “Take the yoke off”, but “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me” (Matt. 11:29). A yoke was the wooden frame laid across two oxen’s necks so they could pull a plough together. Rabbis of the time also used “yoke” for their teaching and rules, which left people gasping for breath. Jesus says, “my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30).

Picture moving house and carrying a fridge. Two amateurs will fumble, strain and end up with aching backs. But if one end is held by a seasoned removals man, he sets the angle, calls the count and takes the weight; you simply follow his rhythm. Jesus’ yoke is like that. It does not mean you never work again; it means you work shoulder to shoulder with him. He carries the weight; he sets the direction. You may still have the same job and the same KPIs, but with a different yoke the same road feels different.

We are often worn out not only by the workload but by carrying others’ expectations, our own perfectionism, the pressure to prove ourselves: these are the yokes of self-centredness. Jesus says, “I am gentle and humble in heart.” He has nothing to prove, so his burden is light. To learn from him is to lay down the weight of wanting to be seen and wanting to be in charge, to share his yoke, and to find rest along the way.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Use your heart, and you find joy; use only your head, and you find worry. Relying on yourself puts every burden on your own shoulders; relying on the Spirit means sharing a yoke with Jesus. Humility is not weakness; it lets the Lord carry the weight.
lessons.scene: Joy works in human resources at a multinational in Singapore. This quarter she is responsible for redundancy interviews with forty people. Every evening her chest feels heavy, and at home she cannot sleep. Today she has six more interviews. In the lift she looks at herself in the mirror and feels she is about to give way.
q: Who is God? — Jesus says he is “gentle and humble in heart”. Is that the Jesus you picture?
Who am I? — Of the yokes on your shoulders now, which are from God, and which have you or others added?
How shall I respond? — Before Joy walks into the interview room today, how can she share this yoke with Jesus?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is not a coach shouting “Keep going!” from a distance. He carried the heaviest cross himself, up to Golgotha. He bore our sin and our burdens, so he has every right to say, “Come to me.” His invitation is signed with his own wounds.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, gentle and humble, I am so tired. I confess I have carried many burdens that are not mine: other people’s opinions, perfect standards, the anxiety of proving myself. Today I lay them at your feet. I will take your yoke and learn from you. In my heaviest meetings, be with me and carry the weight. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down one burden that isn’t mine; give it to the Lord
Before the hardest meeting, pray: Lord, together
If I can’t sleep or cope for long, talk to someone I trust
lessons.noon: “Come to me, all you who labour and are heavily burdened” — Lord, right now I come to you and set my burden down.

lessons.title: Pull Down the Shutter
lessons.theme: Draw lines around rest to guard time with God and others

v: “Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as the LORD your God commanded you.
You shall labour six days, and do all your work;

but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God, in which you shall not do any work— neither you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your ox, nor your donkey, nor any of your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; that your male servant and your female servant may rest as well as you.

You shall remember that you were a servant in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God brought you out of there by a mighty hand and by an outstretched arm. Therefore the LORD your God commanded you to keep the Sabbath day.
There remains therefore a Sabbath rest for the people of God.
For he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his.

lessons.still: Before work, picture the moment you finish today. Say to the Lord: “Lord, help me finish on time today, put down what needs putting down, and keep the evening for you and the people I love.”
teach: When Deuteronomy restates the Ten Commandments, it gives a new reason for the Sabbath: “You shall remember that you were a servant in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God brought you out of there by a mighty hand and by an outstretched arm” (Deut. 5:15). Slaves cannot rest; being able to stop is itself a mark of the free. Hebrews goes further: “There remains therefore a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Heb. 4:9). The Sabbath is a preview: one day we will enjoy eternal rest in God’s presence.

The noodle shop on the corner pulls down its metal shutter at nine o’clock sharp. The owner is not uninterested in money; he knows he has to open again tomorrow. The shutter protects not only the stock inside but the owner’s family and health. The trouble with modern work is that we have no shutter. The phone is on twenty-four hours a day, messages arrive at any moment, and the living room has become an office. Setting boundaries means fitting yourself a shutter: when it comes down, which messages wait until tomorrow, and what genuinely counts as urgent.

Boundaries need to be concrete: a fixed time, a switch-off action, a clear sentence to your colleagues. Some jobs make Sunday impossible; then choose another day as your Sabbath. What matters is not which day but that you have “rested from his works” (Heb. 4:10), giving that day to God, to family and to renewal. If workplace demands keep crossing the line and affecting your health, talk with someone you trust and seek professional help where needed.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Boundaries around rest guard exactly that order of life and relationships. Building a godly system starts with my own weekly timetable, letting Jesus be King.
lessons.scene: Haitao is an operations manager at an e-commerce company in Shenzhen. His boss habitually drops tasks into the group chat at eleven at night, and everyone replies within seconds. Haitao wants to start turning off work notifications all day on Saturdays to be with his children and go to church, but he fears being seen as not committed. On Friday evening he opens a draft announcement to his team and cannot write the first line.
q: Who is God? — God brought Israel out of slavery. What freedom does he want you to enjoy in your work?
Who am I? — Do you have a “shutter” in your life? Where does it most often fail?
How shall I respond? — How can Haitao explain his boundary to his team gently and clearly?
lessons.jesus: Jesus was mobbed by crowds who all wanted him, yet again and again “he went up into the mountain by himself to pray”. He healed many, and he also told his disciples, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” His boundaries were not an escape from his mission; they served to fulfil it more completely.
lessons.pray: Lord who sets me free, thank you for bringing me out of slavery to work. Give me wisdom and courage to draw clear boundaries around rest, and gentle words to explain them to my colleagues. When messages ping in the night, remind me that you are still in charge. Let my timetable, too, show that you are King. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Set a daily time to switch off work notifications
Fix this week’s Sabbath and write it in my calendar
Explain my boundary to my team in one gentle sentence
lessons.noon: “he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works” — Lord, right now I lay down my work and enter your rest.

mem.t: casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.

lessons.title: The Loading Bay
lessons.theme: Cast all your worries on God, because he cares for you

v: Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time,
casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.
Cast your burden on the LORD and he will sustain you. He will never allow the righteous to be moved.

lessons.still: Before work, think of the thing you are most worried about today. Clench your fists, then slowly open them. Say to the Lord: “Lord, I can’t hold this. I cast it on you, because you care for me.”
teach: Peter was writing to believers scattered and under pressure. He did not tell them, “Don’t overthink it.” He gave them an action: “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you” (1 Pet. 5:7). The word “cast” means to throw something onto, like heaving a pack onto a donkey’s back. Notice the verse before: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God” (1 Pet. 5:6). Casting off worry and humility belong together. David says the same: “Cast your burden on the LORD and he will sustain you” (Ps. 55:22).

A logistics warehouse has a loading bay. A lorry reverses up, the rear doors open, and the goods are unloaded, checked and taken into stock. No driver takes a full load home overnight, or he could not go out again the next day. Yet many hearts are like a lorry that never unloads: yesterday’s complaint, last week’s appraisal, next month’s mortgage, all piled in the back, getting heavier with every mile. God is a loading bay that never closes, and he signs for every delivery himself.

Why does unloading require humility? Because clinging to worry is often the self-centred heart saying, “Only I can handle this; I must control the outcome.” Worry can be a hidden pride, as though I knew better than God what should happen. Humility admits that I am human and he is God; his hand is mighty and his heart cares for me. Casting is not shirking responsibility. It is handing the outcome to the one who can truly bear it.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility means laying down power and returning to my place, letting people be people and God be God. Worry is often an attempt to replace God in controlling the future; casting it on him lets Jesus be King. When our focus turns from the problem back to Jesus, the heart finds rest.
lessons.scene: Jingyi works in sales for an export factory in Kaohsiung. Their biggest European client has suddenly said it will review its suppliers and will not give an answer until next month. That order is thirty per cent of the company’s revenue, and her boss asks for updates every day. She wakes at two in the morning, replaying every email she has exchanged with the client.
q: Who is God? — “Because he cares for you.” Do you believe God cares about the small thing you are worried about today?
Who am I? — What kind of worry do you most often take home overnight?
How shall I respond? — How can Jingyi follow up responsibly today while casting the outcome on God?
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane Jesus said, “My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death.” He did not pretend to be strong. He fell on his face and poured out his burden to the Father: “not what I desire, but what you desire.” He went through the deepest anguish himself, and showed us what true entrusting looks like.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father who cares for me, I confess that I grip my worries tightly, as though thinking hard enough could make things go my way. Today I cast on you the thing that keeps me awake. Give me wisdom to do what I should do, and peace to let go of what I cannot control. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down today’s biggest worry and pray over it
Write the next concrete step; leave the rest to God
Before going home, pray an “unloading prayer”
lessons.noon: “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you” — Lord, right now I cast this matter in my hands on you.

lessons.title: Pit Stop under the Juniper
lessons.theme: When you are exhausted, God first feeds you and lets you sleep

v: When he saw that, he arose and ran for his life, and came to Beersheba, which belongs to Judah, and left his servant there.

But he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness, and came and sat down under a juniper tree. Then he requested for himself that he might die, and said, “It is enough. Now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers.”
He lay down and slept under a juniper tree; and behold, an angel touched him, and said to him, “Arise and eat!”
He looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on the coals, and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and lay down again.
The LORD’s angel came again the second time, and touched him, and said, “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.”
He arose, and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb, God’s Mountain.

lessons.still: Before work, drink a glass of water slowly, all the way to the end. Say to the Lord: “Lord, you are the God who gave Elijah bread and water. I am tired today too. Please refuel me yourself.”
teach: Elijah had just seen God’s mighty victory on Mount Carmel, yet one threat from Jezebel sent him fleeing into the wilderness, where he sat under a juniper tree and asked to die: “It is enough. Now, O LORD, take away my life” (1 Kgs 19:4). God did not rebuke him, nor did he immediately hand him a spiritual lecture. God let him sleep, then sent an angel to touch him: “Arise and eat!” (1 Kgs 19:5). He ate and slept again, and the angel came a second time: “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you” (1 Kgs 19:7).

Anyone who has run a marathon knows how vital the refreshment stations are. However fast you start, if you do not stop for water and energy, you will hit the wall in the second half. Elijah’s problem was not too little faith; he had run an extremely intense stage with no refuelling. It happens at work all the time: just after a major project, a run of night shifts, or the year-end close, someone collapses right after their greatest “success”. That is not spiritual failure. It is your body and soul telling you it is time for a pit stop.

God’s order of care for Elijah is tender: body first, then soul, then mission. Only later, at Horeb, did he ask, “What are you doing here, Elijah?” The self-centred heart thinks it is the last one standing: “I, even I only, am left.” But God showed him there were still seven thousand. You are not fighting alone. If you have persistent thoughts of hopelessness or of not wanting to live, please reach out to someone you trust straight away, and seek professional help.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Use your heart and rely on the Spirit, not your head and yourself. Relying on yourself means holding on alone until you collapse; relying on the Spirit means admitting weakness and accepting care. In 235, a spiritual companion is often the angel God sends to tap you on the shoulder.
lessons.scene: Bolin is a resident doctor at a hospital in Tainan. He has just finished a thirty-hour shift and been told he must cover A&E next week. He sits in his car in the car park without starting the engine, wanting only to close his eyes and not open them again. On his phone, a brother from his church small group has sent a message: “How are you doing lately?”
q: Who is God? — Faced with Elijah longing to die, God first provided bread and water. What does that show you about his heart?
Who am I? — Do you tend to collapse right after a victory? Where is your refreshment station?
How shall I respond? — How could Bolin reply to that message and let himself be cared for?
lessons.jesus: Jesus also grew tired. “Jesus therefore, being tired from his journey, sat down by the well.” He slept on a cushion in the stern of the boat, and he took his disciples away to rest. After rising from the dead, he lit a charcoal fire on the shore and made breakfast for his weary disciples. His care for people so often begins with a meal.
lessons.pray: Lord who cared for Elijah, I am so tired; sometimes I don’t want to keep going. Thank you that you do not scold my weakness but set out bread and water. Today make me willing to stop, to eat, to sleep, and to accept other people’s care. I am not alone: you are here, and so is your family. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Eat a proper lunch today away from my screen
Go to bed an hour earlier tonight
Reply honestly to someone who has asked how I am
lessons.noon: “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.” — Lord, right now I receive your refuelling. Strengthen me.

lessons.title: One Delivery at a Time
lessons.theme: Give tomorrow to God and give yourself to today

v: “Therefore don’t be anxious, saying, ‘What will we eat?’, ‘What will we drink?’ or, ‘With what will we be clothed?’
For the Gentiles seek after all these things; for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things.
But seek first God’s Kingdom and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.
Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient.

lessons.still: Before work, close your eyes and think only of today. Say to the Lord: “Lord, tomorrow has not come, and you are already there. Today I just want to follow you and walk this one day well.”
teach: In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus says, “don’t be anxious, saying, ‘What will we eat?’, ‘What will we drink?’ or, ‘With what will we be clothed?’” (Matt. 6:31). He is not saying these things do not matter, but that “your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things” (Matt. 6:32). Then he gives the order: “seek first God’s Kingdom and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” Finally comes a very practical word: “don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient” (Matt. 6:34).

An experienced delivery rider may have several orders pinging on his phone at once, but he knows that on the road he can only give his attention to one delivery at a time. If he rides along thinking about the next order and the one after that, he is likely to jump a red light or go to the wrong address. Our minds are often delivering the presentation due in three days, next month’s appraisal and next year’s redundancy rumours all at once, and today’s delivery ends up in a mess. Jesus teaches us to bring our minds back to today’s road.

Worrying about tomorrow is trying to live in a day that has not yet come, and to live it without the grace that will be given for it. God’s grace is issued daily, like manna. This is not a call to stop planning. Planning is today’s work; worry is trying to carry tomorrow’s load. Keep the focus on Jesus, not on circumstances: he is with me today, and he is already there tomorrow.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Shift perspective from the temporary to the eternal, from the earthly to the heavenly. Seek his Kingdom first; when the order is right, worry finds its proper place. Focus on Jesus, not tomorrow’s circumstances, and let him be King of today and of tomorrow.
lessons.scene: Wanrong works at an accountancy firm in Singapore. Early next year she sits her professional exams, and rumours are going round that her department will be merged. Today she has been staring at a spreadsheet for twenty minutes and is still on the first page, her mind rehearsing: what if I fail? What if I’m made redundant? Her manager walks past and asks if the report is ready.
q: Who is God? — “Your heavenly Father knows.” How does that comfort you in your present anxiety?
Who am I? — Which tomorrow that has not yet happened do you worry about most?
How shall I respond? — How can Wanrong bring her mind back to today’s spreadsheet?
lessons.jesus: Jesus knew the cross lay ahead, yet he was not swallowed up by tomorrow. Each day he gave himself fully to healing, teaching and being with the people before him: stopping for a woman who had bled for years, taking children in his arms, eating at Zacchaeus’ house. He entrusted tomorrow wholly to the Father, so he could live wholly in today.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, you know all I need. I confess I often carry tomorrow’s load today, and then today’s work is done badly too. Help me to seek your Kingdom first, place tomorrow in your hands, and give myself to the one task in front of me. Thank you that your grace is enough for each day. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: List today’s three most important tasks; start the first
When a worry surfaces, note it for “tomorrow’s prayer”
Before leaving, thank God that today’s grace was enough
lessons.noon: “Each day’s own evil is sufficient.” — Lord, right now I just want to follow you and take the next step well.

lessons.title: Warning Lights On
lessons.theme: Caring for your body is stewardship, not weakness

v: Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own,
for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s.
The apostles gathered themselves together to Jesus, and they told him all things, whatever they had done, and whatever they had taught.
He said to them, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” For there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
They went away in the boat to a deserted place by themselves.

lessons.still: Before work, scan your body from head to toe: neck and shoulders, eyes, stomach, breathing. Say to the Lord: “Lord, this body is your temple. Today remind me to look after it well.”
teach: Paul writes, “don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:19–20). The body is not a burden on the soul but a temple entrusted by God. When the apostles returned from their mission eager to report, Jesus said, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” Scripture notes the reason: “they had no leisure so much as to eat” (Mark 6:31).

When a red light comes on in your car’s dashboard — low oil, engine overheating, low tyre pressure — a sensible driver does not cover it with tape and drive on. Burnout has warning lights too: long-term insomnia, stomach aches and headaches, impatience with family, dread starting on Sunday evening, losing interest in things you once loved. Many Christians cover those lights with tape and call it “giving my all for the Lord”, when in fact they are wearing out God’s temple. Seeing Moses judging from morning to evening, his father-in-law said, “the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to perform it yourself alone” (Exod. 18:18).

Refusing to care for the body is sometimes self-centredness: I must prove I am useful; I cannot let anyone down. A good steward knows the body is not mine but the Lord’s; I am not a perpetual-motion machine but a creature. Caring for the body is a spiritual discipline: sleep, exercise, meals and doctor’s appointments can all be worship. If the warning lights have been on for a long time, please do not push on alone. Talk with someone you trust, and seek medical or professional help.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is God, then myself, then others, then tasks. Looking after myself is not selfishness but a steward’s duty, because the body is the Spirit’s temple. Burning myself out for the sake of tasks also hurts the people around me.
lessons.scene: Jinhui is a partner at an architecture practice in Kuala Lumpur. For eight months he has left the office after midnight every night. Lately he has been getting tightness in his chest, and his health check report arrived two weeks ago, still unopened. Today another tender deadline looms, and a colleague asks, “Staying late with us again tonight?”
q: Who is God? — God says you were “bought with a price”. How does he regard your body?
Who am I? — Which warning lights are on in your dashboard right now?
How shall I respond? — What is the first thing Jinhui could do today to look after his body?
lessons.jesus: The Word became flesh: Jesus had a real body that grew hungry, thirsty and tired, and that wept. He did not despise the body; he gave his body for us on the cross, and his body was raised with him. With his own body he tells us that the body is precious.
lessons.pray: Lord who bought me at great cost, thank you for this body. I confess I often ignore its warnings and treat it as a tool rather than your temple. Give me courage to stop: to see a doctor, to sleep, to eat a proper meal. Let me glorify you in my body. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down one warning light my body is showing
Book that long-postponed check-up or appointment
Walk, stretch or exercise for fifteen minutes today
lessons.noon: “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” — Lord, right now I hear your invitation, and I am willing to rest.

lessons.title: The One-Minute Handover
lessons.theme: Anytime, anywhere, hand your burden to the Lord in one minute

v: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.
Trust in him at all times, you people. Pour out your heart before him. God is a refuge for us.

lessons.still: Before work, set a one-minute timer. For the first twenty seconds, name your worry; for the next twenty, give thanks for one thing; for the last twenty, say: “Lord, I hand it to you. Let your peace guard my heart.”
teach: From prison Paul wrote, “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God” (Phil. 4:6). Notice the thanksgiving: not after the problem is solved, but at the very moment of entrusting. The result: “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus” (Phil. 4:7). David also invites us: “Trust in him at all times, you people. Pour out your heart before him. God is a refuge for us” (Ps. 62:8).

Hospital nurses hand over at every change of shift: each patient’s condition, medication and points to watch, passed on clearly to the next team. A good handover lets the next shift take over and lets the last shift go home in peace. It need not be long, but it must be clear and specific. We can learn a one-minute handover prayer: clearly passing to the Lord the one thing troubling me, and then truly letting go and letting him take the next shift. He is the one who never dozes off.

This week we have learned to cast off worry, accept refuelling, live in today and care for our bodies. Today we turn it into a habit we can carry anywhere: the minute before a meeting, the minute before answering a difficult email, the minute you step out of the office. Entrusting is not a one-off; it takes repeated practice, like the steps of practice and repetition among the eight steps. Every handover is a declaration that Jesus is King.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The eight steps of a changed mindset are information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition and multiplication. The one-minute handover prayer turns “casting it on God” into practice and repetition, until it becomes a habit of life.
lessons.scene: Oliver teaches maths at a secondary school in Wellington and is also a student counsellor. Just before period three, he takes a furious phone call from a parent, and next he must walk into a classroom of thirty pupils. In the corridor, he has one minute left.
q: Who is God? — God is “a refuge for us”. When have you known his peace guarding your heart?
Who am I? — At what moments in your day do you most need a one-minute handover?
How shall I respond? — In that minute in the corridor, how could Oliver hand over to the Lord?
lessons.jesus: Even on his busiest days, Jesus rose before dawn to pray. At Lazarus’ tomb he lifted up his eyes and said, “Father, I thank you that you listened to me.” Sometimes his prayers were long, sometimes a single sentence, but he was always connected to the Father, and so he always carried peace.
lessons.pray: Lord of peace, thank you that you hear my prayers at any moment. Today, in every tense moment, remind me to stop for a minute and hand my burden over to you. I thank you that you have already heard me, and I trust you to take over. Let your peace, which surpasses understanding, guard my heart and mind. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Set three phone alarms as one-minute handover reminders
Pray a handover prayer before my tensest meeting
Teach the one-minute handover to a colleague or family member
lessons.noon: “Pour out your heart before him. God is a refuge for us.” — Lord, right now I tell you everything on my heart.

mem.t: It is vain for you to rise up early, to stay up late, eating the bread of toil, for he gives sleep to his loved ones.

lessons.title: Sweat on the Treadmill
lessons.theme: Unless the Lord builds, all our striving is in vain

v: Unless the LORD builds the house, they who build it labour in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.
It is vain for you to rise up early, to stay up late, eating the bread of toil, for he gives sleep to his loved ones.

lessons.still: Before work, stand still with both feet planted firmly. Say to the Lord: “Lord, the business, family and team I am building today are in vain unless you build them. Be today’s chief architect.”
teach: Solomon was the greatest builder in Israel’s history: temple, palace, city walls, trade caravans. Yet he wrote this psalm: “Unless the LORD builds the house, they who build it labour in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain” (Ps. 127:1). Then, more bluntly: “It is vain for you to rise up early, to stay up late, eating the bread of toil, for he gives sleep to his loved ones” (Ps. 127:2). The second half of the psalm turns to children; house and household have always belonged together.

A treadmill at the gym can leave you dripping with sweat and your heart racing. The screen says you have run ten kilometres, but look up and you are still in the same spot. Many working lives are like that treadmill: out early and home late every day, sales figures constantly ticking over, while the house at home is not being built. The children grow more distant, husband and wife say less and less, and your own heart grows drier. The problem is not that you are not working hard enough; it is who is doing the building.

“He gives sleep to his loved ones” can also be read as: God gives to those he loves even while they sleep. This is the gentlest challenge to the self-centred heart. You think everything is held up by your toil, but in fact God is the builder. Letting Jesus be King does not mean you stop working. It means you work within his building, and can also stop, go home and sleep in peace.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Building God’s order begins with letting God be the chief architect. Humility means returning to my place: I am a worker; he is the builder. Shift perspective from human toil to God’s building, from temporary results to an eternal home.
lessons.scene: Zhenbang opened a bubble-tea shop in Ipoh, and in three years it has grown into a chain of nine. Every day he inspects the shops from six in the morning and is still doing the accounts at midnight. Last week he missed his son’s parents’ evening again. Tonight his wife messages: “How long has it been since you had dinner with us?” He is about to sign the lease for shop number ten.
q: Who is God? — God is the one who builds the house and watches over the city. What does he want to build in your home?
Who am I? — Is your effort more like building a house, or running on a treadmill?
How shall I respond? — What questions does Zhenbang need to answer before he signs the lease?
lessons.jesus: Jesus asked, “what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his life?” He too is a builder; he said he would build his church on the rock. He did not build by frantic effort but by obedience to the Father. On the cross, with his own body, he built a house that will never fall: the household of God.
lessons.pray: Lord who builds all things, I confess I often think everything depends on my toil, and I end up exhausted on a treadmill. Be the chief architect of my work and my family. Today, when I plan to expand, work late or take on more, remind me to ask you first: is this what you are building? Let me, too, sleep in peace. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down three things I am currently “building”
For each, ask: is God building this?
Go home on time tonight and enjoy a meal with family
lessons.noon: “for he gives sleep to his loved ones” — Lord, right now I trust that you are building, and I can be at peace.

lessons.title: System, Connection, Apps
lessons.theme: Life first, then relationships, then ministry; order shapes fruit

v: He went up into the mountain and called to himself those whom he wanted, and they went to him.
He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach
and to have authority to heal sicknesses and to cast out demons:
Remain in me, and I in you. As the branch can’t bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me.
I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.

lessons.still: Before work, don’t open any work windows yet. Simply be with the Lord for thirty seconds. Say: “Lord, today I am your child first, and only then an employee, a manager or a boss.”
teach: When Jesus chose the Twelve, the order was very clear: “He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach” (Mark 3:14). First “with him”, then “send them out”. At the Last Supper he said, “Remain in me, and I in you … apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:4–5). The fruit of ministry grows out of a life connected to him.

A smartphone has three layers: the operating system, the network connection and the apps. Even the best app will not open if the operating system crashes, and without a connection many features stop working. Our spiritual life is like the operating system; our relationships with God and others are the connection; our work and ministry are the apps. Many people keep downloading new apps — a new role, a new project, a new ministry — but rarely update the operating system, and barely notice that the connection has been patchy for months.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry: this does not mean perfecting your life before you are allowed to work. It is the order of each day. In the morning, connect with the Lord first; then notice the people around you; only then turn to the task list. The self-centred prove themselves through what they do; the self-emptied draw their identity from their relationship with the Lord, and their work becomes fruit that naturally flows out. Get the order right, and the same work bears different fruit.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry; the order of relationships is God, myself, others, tasks. Five changes from the inside out: when the mindset changes, life changes, and so do lifestyle, relationships and ministry.
lessons.scene: Fengyi is a project manager at a consultancy in Shanghai, and at church she leads children’s Sunday school and a small group. Her diary is packed every day, but lately she has noticed she prays less and less, and she is always rushed when talking with her husband. This week her firm asked her to take on a new client, and the church asked her to start a new ministry.
q: Who is God? — Jesus first called his disciples to “be with him”. What does that show he values most?
Who am I? — How have your “operating system” and “connection” been running lately?
How shall I respond? — Facing two new invitations, how can Fengyi choose in the right order?
lessons.jesus: Before his public ministry, Jesus spent many years in Nazareth, obedient to his parents. During his ministry, one of the things he did most often was withdraw to a quiet place to be with the Father. He said, “Even as the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love.” His ministry flowed out of the Father’s love.
lessons.pray: Lord, the true vine, I confess I often turn the order upside down: ministry first, relationships next, and you last of all. Help me today to remain in you first, then to see the people around me, and only then to start work. Apart from you I can do nothing. Let everything I do flow out of your love. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before switching on my computer, read and pray for three minutes
This morning, ask a colleague or family member how they are
Review this week’s diary; drop or postpone one commitment
lessons.noon: “He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit” — Lord, right now I come back to remain in you.

lessons.title: The House of Eli
lessons.theme: However long you hold a post, losing your home is still failure

v: A man of God came to Eli and said to him, “The LORD says, ‘Did I reveal myself to the house of your father when they were in Egypt in bondage to Pharaoh’s house?

Didn’t I choose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest, to go up to my altar, to burn incense, to wear an ephod before me? Didn’t I give to the house of your father all the offerings of the children of Israel made by fire?

Why do you kick at my sacrifice and at my offering, which I have commanded in my habitation, and honour your sons above me, to make yourselves fat with the best of all the offerings of Israel my people?’
The LORD said to Samuel, “Behold, I will do a thing in Israel at which both the ears of everyone who hears it will tingle.
In that day I will perform against Eli all that I have spoken concerning his house, from the beginning even to the end.
For I have told him that I will judge his house forever for the iniquity which he knew, because his sons brought a curse on themselves, and he didn’t restrain them.

lessons.still: Before work, think of each person in your household. For each name say, “Lord, keep them.” Then say: “Lord, help me to be faithful at work, and not to neglect my duty at home.”
teach: Eli was high priest and judged Israel for forty years. He served at the sanctuary in Shiloh and personally raised Samuel. From the outside, it was a stable and respected ministry. Yet Scripture says Eli’s sons were wicked and did not know the LORD (1 Sam. 2:12). God sent a man of God to confront Eli: why do you “honour your sons above me” (1 Sam. 2:29)? And he told Samuel he would judge Eli’s house “for the iniquity which he knew, because his sons brought a curse on themselves, and he didn’t restrain them” (1 Sam. 3:13).

Some companies publish beautiful annual reports, with record revenue and a healthy share price, while their cash flow has quietly run dry. Then one day they collapse and everyone is stunned. Eli’s house was like that: the lamp in the sanctuary burned every day, while the foundations at home were crumbling. Eli’s problem was not just busyness; he knew, and he did nothing. He chose to keep up a surface peace in his position rather than have the hard conversations at home. Many people handle conflict decisively at work, yet at home they choose to avoid it.

We can imagine that Eli perhaps thought, “I am serving God, so God will look after my family.” But God did not rank family below ministry. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: home is the first and most real field of ministry. This is not meant to load us with guilt, for children ultimately make their own choices. It is an invitation to go home today and, with love and truth, have the conversations that need to be had.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Do not hurt your family for the sake of ministry, or damage relationships for the sake of a position. Let Jesus be King of my home, not only of my office.
lessons.scene: Aroha is chief executive of a charity in Auckland that serves struggling families, and she is often invited to speak. Lately her sixteen-year-old son’s grades have plummeted, and he often comes home after midnight. Last night his teacher phoned, and Aroha agreed to meet after school today — which clashes with an important fundraising meeting.
q: Who is God? — God said to Eli, “you honour your sons above me.” What does he care about?
Who am I? — At home, is there something you “know about but have not dealt with”?
How shall I respond? — How should Aroha arrange this afternoon? Whom could she ask to share the load?
lessons.jesus: When the disciples thought the children a nuisance, Jesus was moved with indignation: “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them.” In the agony of the cross he still remembered his mother and entrusted her to the disciple he loved. In Jesus’ eyes, no mission is so great that it swallows up family.
lessons.pray: Father in heaven, thank you for my family. I confess I often give my best time and strength to work and ministry, and come home with nothing left but tiredness and silence. Give me courage to face the conversations I have been avoiding, and wisdom to walk with my family in love and truth. Be King in my home. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down one family issue I have been avoiding
Set aside fifteen focused minutes with one family member
Pray one specific sentence for each person at home
lessons.noon: “honour your sons above me” — Lord, right now reorder my heart, and take first place.

lessons.title: The Pop-Up Dinner Table
lessons.theme: Some moments never return; the table is a place of service too

v: These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart;
and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.
So when they got out on the land, they saw a fire of coals there, with fish and bread laid on it.
Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish which you have just caught.”
Simon Peter went up, and drew the net to land, full of one hundred and fifty-three great fish. Even though there were so many, the net wasn’t torn.
Jesus said to them, “Come and eat breakfast!” None of the disciples dared enquire of him, “Who are you?” knowing that it was the Lord.

lessons.still: Before work, picture tonight’s dinner table at home, or wherever you eat with flatmates or friends. Say to the Lord: “Lord, help me leave the meeting table on time today, and bring your presence back to that table.”
teach: God commanded Israel: “These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart; and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up” (Deut. 6:6–7). Passing on faith did not happen once a week in the synagogue but in the everyday life of the home. After his resurrection, Jesus lit a charcoal fire on the shore of the Sea of Tiberias, cooked fish and bread, and said to disciples who had caught nothing all night, “Come and eat breakfast!” (John 21:12). The risen Lord himself prepared a meal.

Shopping centres often host pop-up shops: open for two weeks, then gone, and if you miss them you miss out. A child’s years at home, a parent’s final years, the seasons when husband and wife still have energy to really talk — they are all pop-ups. They will not stay open for ever. A meeting can be rescheduled and a report can go in tomorrow, but the evening your child first wants to share what is on their heart will not come round again in quite the same way. Not every meeting is unimportant; the point is to discern which table needs me more tonight.

The self-centred heart often thinks, “If I’m not there, the company will have problems.” But your family does not need your achievements; they need your presence. Of course, some jobs require night shifts or travel; then create your own “table time” in other slots. Letting Jesus be King means letting him decide which table I sit at tonight, and sitting down there with his peace.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. The dinner table is an altar of relationship; people matter more than tasks. Shift perspective: what is achieved at the meeting table is temporary, but the life and faith built at the dinner table are eternal.
lessons.scene: Jianzhong is head of research and development at a tech company in Taichung. He promised his daughter he would have dinner with her tonight and hear which universities she is thinking about. At six o’clock the vice-president calls an emergency meeting, and everyone looks at him: “You’ll be staying, won’t you?” On his phone, his daughter has just sent a photo of the table already laid.
q: Who is God? — The risen Jesus lit a fire and made breakfast for his disciples. What does that show you about his heart?
Who am I? — What is the “pop-up” in your home? Which moment would you least want to miss?
How shall I respond? — How could Jianzhong answer the vice-president sincerely while keeping his promise to his daughter?
lessons.jesus: Jesus so often worked at the table: at the wedding in Cana, at Zacchaeus’ house, at the home of Martha and Mary, at the Last Supper. He said, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.” He turned the table into a place where grace arrives, and he invites us back to our own tables.
lessons.pray: Lord who made breakfast for your disciples on the shore, thank you for valuing time at the table. I confess I often let the meeting table crowd out the dinner table at home. Give me wisdom to discern when to stay and when to go home, and courage to state my commitments honestly and gently. Let my table, too, be a place where your grace arrives. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Choose three evenings this week to be home for dinner
At the table, put my phone away and ask a good question
After dinner, pray together about one thing
lessons.noon: “Come and eat breakfast!” — Lord, right now I hear your invitation; may I sit beside my family tonight.

lessons.title: The 23-Kilogram Suitcase
lessons.theme: Redistribute the week’s hours in God’s order

v: For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:
a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted;
a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;
a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;
a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away;
a time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak;
a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.

lessons.still: Before work, open this week’s calendar, but don’t rush to fill it. Say to the Lord: “Lord, all one hundred and sixty-eight hours are yours. Teach me to put in what matters most first, and everything else after.”
teach: The Teacher says, “For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven” (Eccl. 3:1). He goes on to list fourteen pairs of opposites: a time to plant and a time to pluck up; a time to break down and a time to build up; a time to weep and a time to laugh; “a time to keep silence, and a time to speak” (Eccl. 3:7). Life is not everything at once; different seasons call for different things. Wisdom is not cramming every minute full, but knowing what this moment is the time for.

When you fly abroad, your checked baggage allowance might be twenty-three kilograms. Overweight, and you have to open your suitcase at the check-in desk and painfully decide what to take out. A wise traveller packs at home with the essentials first: passport, medicine, a change of clothes, and souvenirs squeezed in last. Our week also has a fixed weight: one hundred and sixty-eight hours. If work and social obligations go in first, sleep, worship, family and friends get squeezed out, and we end up scrambling at the check-in desk every weekend.

In this unit we have learned about rest, entrusting, and the order of work and family. Today we turn it into a timetable: first put in time with God and the Sabbath, then sleep and family, then work, and finally everything else. You will not keep it perfectly; the point is to practise, review, correct and repeat, as in the eight steps. A timetable reveals who is King. Letting Jesus be King starts with next week’s calendar.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is God, myself, others, tasks. The steps of practice, review and correction among the eight steps turn that order into a weekly timetable. Building God’s order begins with redistributing my one hundred and sixty-eight hours.
lessons.scene: Ziqian left his job in Suzhou to care at home for their two children and his elderly mother-in-law, while his wife works for a foreign firm. His day runs from half past five in the morning to eleven at night: shopping, school runs, hospital appointments, cooking. Yet he often feels he has achieved nothing. Tonight, with the children asleep, he opens a notebook to plan a new timetable for next week, but does not know where to begin.
q: Who is God? — God has set a time for every purpose under heaven. How does that shape the way you see your limited time?
Who am I? — Looking at last week, what went into your “suitcase”, and what got squeezed out?
How shall I respond? — Which most important things could Ziqian put into next week’s timetable first?
lessons.jesus: Jesus’ days on earth were limited, yet he was never flustered: a time to heal, a time to teach, a time to pray alone, a time to feast, a time to rest. He knew the times the Father had set for him, and on the cross he finished everything. To follow him is to learn to arrange my time in his rhythm and his order.
lessons.pray: Lord who sets a time for everything, thank you for entrusting this week’s hours to me. I confess I often let work and chores fill everything first, and push you, my family and my body to the end. Teach me today to reorder, putting first what matters most. Let my calendar bear witness that you are King of my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Note roughly where my hours went last week
Schedule devotions, Sabbath and family time first
Remove one commitment to make room for what matters
lessons.noon: “For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven” — Lord, right now show me what this moment is for.

mem.t: Honour the LORD with your substance, with the first fruits of all your increase.

lessons.title: Everything Has an Owner
lessons.theme: All that passes through my hands is God's; I am only the steward

v: The earth is the LORD’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell in it.
For he has founded it on the seas, and established it on the floods.
But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly as this? For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own.

lessons.still: Sit still and rest your open hands on your knees. Say to the Lord: “Lord, my salary, my time, my skills, even this desk — they are all yours. Today I am not the owner; I am the one who handles them for you.” Then slowly close your hands and begin your work in trust.
teach: David opens Psalm 24 by registering the title deed of the whole universe: “The earth is the LORD’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell in it” (Ps 24:1). The reason is simple — he founded it on the seas. Late in life David gathered vast amounts of gold and silver for the temple, and the leaders of Israel gave willingly. It was one of Israel’s finest hours. Yet when David prayed, he did not boast of his generosity. He said, “All things come from you, and we have given you of your own” (1 Chr 29:14). For David, giving was not handing God what was ours, but returning to God what was his.

Picture a bank teller. In a single day she may handle more cash than she earns in ten years. She counts, checks and records it with practised care. Yet she would never call the money in her drawer “my money”, because every note belongs to someone else’s account. For the Christian at work, the payslip, the client’s budget, the company’s equipment and even our professional skills are all registered in God’s name. We are tellers, not account holders. Our dignity lies not in how much we own, but in whether we handle it faithfully, clearly and with a clean ledger.

The root of the fall is quietly changing “handling” into “owning”. The self-centred life says, “I worked hard for this, so I can spend it however I like.” It sounds reasonable, but it quietly erases God’s name from the books. Change your thinking and your life will change: when I confess that everything belongs to God, money steps down from master to servant, and I step down from anxious owner to settled steward. Letting Jesus be King begins by handing the title deed back to him. I no longer have to carry the weight of “it all depends on me”, because the true Owner takes responsibility to the end.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Shift your perspective — from the human view to God’s view, from “mine” to “his”. Humility means laying down power and returning to my proper place: God is the Owner, I am the steward. That one change of position transforms how I see every pay cheque.
lessons.scene: Ziqing is in her third year as a dental assistant, and has just received her first year-end bonus worth two months’ pay. At lunch she opens her banking app, her finger hovering over “Transfer all to investment account” — a colleague says this fund can’t lose. Suddenly she realises she has not prayed about this money once, or even asked whom it belongs to.
q: Who is God? — Psalm 24 says the earth and its fullness belong to the LORD. What does that show you about who God is in your financial life?
Who am I? — Are you more like an account holder or a teller? What is the hardest thing for you to admit is “not mine”?
How shall I respond? — If you were Ziqing, what would you do before pressing that button?
lessons.jesus: All things were made through Jesus (John 1:3); the whole world was his estate. Yet at his birth he was laid “in a feeding trough, because there was no room for them in the inn” (Luke 2:7). All his life “the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt 8:20), and at his death soldiers gambled for his clothes. The Owner of all things willingly owned nothing, so that we who had seized God’s property might be bought back by him.
lessons.pray: Lord of heaven and earth, the earth and its fullness are yours. I confess that I often treat my salary as my trophy and my abilities as my own capital. Today I hand the title deed back to you: my income, my time and every budget I handle at work are in your name. Teach me to be a faithful, clear-headed and unanxious steward. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write “The LORD’s” beside your payslip or account page
Pray for faithfulness over one company budget you handle today
Tell God in one sentence: “This isn’t mine; it’s yours.”
lessons.noon: “The earth is the LORD’s, with its fullness” — Lord, right now I open my grasping hands and rest as your steward.

lessons.title: God on the First Line of the Budget
lessons.theme: How I spend reveals whom I truly honour

v: Honour the LORD with your substance, with the first fruits of all your increase;
so your barns will be filled with plenty, and your vats will overflow with new wine.

lessons.still: Open your budgeting or banking app. Don’t look at the numbers yet; just pray over it: “Lord, every amount here says whom I honour. Today, may they all say: I honour you.” Then put the phone down and start work.
teach: Proverbs 3 is a father’s counsel to his son: “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding” (Prov 3:5). Then he brings that trust down to the most practical place of all — the wallet: “Honour the LORD with your substance, with the first fruits of all your increase” (Prov 3:9). The Hebrew root of “honour” carries the idea of weight. To honour God is to let him carry the most weight in my life. For a farmer, the first fruits were the first harvest of a whole year’s labour — the fullest, the hardest to let go of, and the clearest proof of where his heart was.

Seasoned investors say that if you want to know a company’s real strategy, ignore the slide deck and read the budget. The presentation can say “customers first” or “we value our people”, but the budget honestly tells you whether the money goes to advertising, to shareholders or to staff training. Faith is the same. It is easy to say “the Lord comes first”, but credit card statements and salary allocations don’t lie. Honouring God with our wealth means putting him on the first line of the budget, not in the “miscellaneous” box at the end of the month.

The promise of verse 10, “your barns will be filled with plenty”, is not a guaranteed return on investment, nor the prosperity gospel of “give a thousand, gain ten thousand”. It describes the abundant order that comes to those who put God first: when God is in charge, provision is no longer an anxiety I carry alone. The change works from the inside out — first God gains weight in my heart (my thinking), then my money follows my heart (my living). When the flow of my money changes, I know that Jesus truly reigns in me, and is not merely an honorary chairman.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus receive all the glory. Honouring God happens not only when we sing on Sunday, but when we make decisions on payday. Change your thinking and your living will change: when God carries the most weight in my heart, my money naturally turns towards him.
lessons.scene: Haoran is a sales manager at a logistics company in Singapore and has just been promoted with a pay rise. One evening he and his wife sit down to plan the new family budget: mortgage, the children’s tuition, a car fund, holidays… At the bottom, his wife asks, “Where does our giving go? Or do we do what we always do — see what’s left at the end of the month?” Haoran holds the pen and can’t bring himself to write.
q: Who is God? — Why is he worthy of my “first fruits”, the very best portion?
Who am I? — If someone looked only at your bank statements, what would they say you honour most?
How shall I respond? — If you were Haoran, on which line of the budget would you write your giving? Why?
lessons.jesus: God the Father did not give us his leftovers; he gave his best, his only Son (John 3:16). Jesus was raised from the dead and “became the first fruit of those who are asleep” (1 Cor 15:20). God first honoured us, the undeserving, with his very best. I offer my first fruits in response — not to purchase a blessing, but because I have already received the greatest blessing of all.
lessons.pray: Father, you did not give me what was left over; you gave me your beloved Son. I confess that I often satisfy myself first and give you the small change. Today I want to reorder my budget so that you are on the first line, not the last. Reorder my heart too, so that you carry the most weight in my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Move giving to the first line of this month’s budget
On your next payday, pray before you transfer
Name one expense you’d hate to cut; let God examine it
lessons.noon: “Honour the LORD with your substance, with the first fruits of all your increase” — Lord, right now let you carry the most weight in my heart.

lessons.title: One Day We Give Account
lessons.theme: Faithfulness in the smallest things is the steward’s exam

v: He also said to his disciples, “There was a certain rich man who had a manager. An accusation was made to him that this man was wasting his possessions.
He called him, and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear about you? Give an accounting of your management, for you can no longer be manager.’
He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.
If therefore you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches?
If you have not been faithful in that which is another’s, who will give you that which is your own?
No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will hold to one and despise the other. You aren’t able to serve God and Mammon.”

lessons.still: Place the first receipt or email of the day in front of you and pray quietly: “Lord, this is a small thing, but you have entrusted it to me too. Let me be faithful to you in this small thing.”
teach: Jesus told a parable that makes us frown. A manager was accused of wasting his master’s possessions. His master said, “Give an accounting of your management, for you can no longer be manager” (Luke 16:2). The manager quickly reduced the debtors’ bills to secure his own future. Jesus was not praising his dishonesty; he was pointing out how shrewd “the children of this world” are about their future (Luke 16:8), while the children of light are often careless about eternity. Then Jesus gave the heart of it: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10). Money is “a very little”, yet it is the exam that shows whether we can be trusted with “the true riches”.

Many companies have internal auditors. They don’t wait for a major scandal; they deliberately sample the smallest documents — a taxi receipt, a meal claim, a stock adjustment — because small things reveal who a person really is. Jesus looks at us the same way: a ten-dollar line on an expense claim, half an hour of company time, the office stationery and photocopier. These are not trivial details; they are heaven’s audit samples. Faithfulness where no one is watching is the only real faithfulness.

Jesus concludes: “You aren’t able to serve God and Mammon” (Luke 16:13). Mammon is not just money; it is a false god that wants the throne. The self-centred heart wants to grip both — serving God on Sunday and serving targets and bank balances the rest of the week. But there is only one throne. Letting Jesus be King means choosing him in the small things every day. Faithfulness is not a personality trait we are born with; it is the fruit the Holy Spirit grows in us as we hand small things to the King, again and again.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Bible is my standard. Faithfulness is fruit of the Spirit — the “9” in 920 (the nine-fold fruit of a self-emptied life towards each person around me) grows from the smallest things. People matter more than tasks, and integrity matters more than targets; never trade a small gain for the trust of the Lord and your colleagues.
lessons.scene: Ruixiang is a field salesman for a building materials company in Malaysia. At month-end a colleague tells him, “Everyone adds a bit to their petrol claims. The boss knows — it’s the unwritten rule.” The claims system is open, and the petrol box is still empty. Ruixiang does the maths: an extra two hundred ringgit would exactly cover his child’s tuition this month.
q: Who is God? — Jesus links the smallest things with great things. How does he view the “small things” of our lives?
Who am I? — Where no one checks the books, what kind of steward are you?
How shall I respond? — Facing the “unwritten rule”, how can Ruixiang be faithful without becoming self-righteous?
lessons.jesus: Jesus never served two masters. On the high mountain the devil showed him the glory of all the kingdoms, all his for a single act of worship. Jesus replied, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only” (Matt 4:10). He served the Father wholeheartedly, all the way to the cross where he said, “It is finished.” He settled the account for us unfaithful managers, and now he lives in us as our strength to be faithful.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the good and faithful one. I confess that I often loosen my grip on small things, telling myself “everyone does it”. Today guard my expense claims, my timesheet and every piece of company property in my hands. When I face unwritten rules, give me courage to say no, and gentleness not to judge others. I want to serve you alone. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Fill in today’s claims or timesheet exactly — not a cent more
Return one company item you took home
Name one “everyone does it” grey area before the Lord
lessons.noon: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” — Lord, right now let me be faithful to you in this small thing.

lessons.title: Faith in the Right Order
lessons.theme: The tithe is not a tax but a practice of putting God first

v: Will a man rob God? Yet you rob me! But you say, ‘How have we robbed you?’ In tithes and offerings.
You are cursed with the curse; for you rob me, even this whole nation.

Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in my house, and test me now in this,” says the LORD of Armies, “if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there will not be enough room for.

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and have left undone the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faith. But you ought to have done these, and not to have left the other undone.

lessons.still: Close your eyes and tap the desk three times, saying silently: “God first, people second, tasks third.” Then say to the Lord, “Please stand at the front of everything I do today.”
