teach: In Malachi’s day the people had returned from exile and the temple had been rebuilt, but their zeal had gone cold. God asked them bluntly, “Will a man rob God? Yet you rob me!” They protested, “How have we robbed you?” God answered, “In tithes and offerings” (Mal 3:8). Then, remarkably, God invited them to “test me now in this” (Mal 3:10). The tithe appears even before the law of Moses: Abram gave Melchizedek “a tenth of all” (Gen 14:20), and Jacob vowed, “I will surely give a tenth to you” (Gen 28:22). At its heart is not just a percentage but an order.

Every IT engineer knows about the boot order. If the system is set to read the wrong drive first, even the best hardware won’t start up. Our financial life has a boot order too. If it reads “what I need” first and “what’s left for God” second, the whole system keeps crashing — anxiety, comparison, never enough. Tithing resets the boot order to the right place: God first. It is not that God is short of money; it is that our hearts need resetting, again and again.

Yet Jesus also warned that the Pharisees tithed “mint, dill, and cumin” but left undone “justice, mercy, and faith” (Matt 23:23). Tithing can become a self-righteous clocking-in, as though paying the membership fee buys peace of mind. Jesus did not abolish the tithe; he said, “you ought to have done these, and not to have left the other undone.” But the heart matters more. Under grace we are not looking to give less; we start from a tenth and grow towards offering everything. When the order is right, the heart falls into line too.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is God, self, others, tasks — and money follows the same order. The tithe turns “God first” from a slogan into an action; our focus is on Jesus, not on the numbers. Lean on the Spirit with your heart, and you won’t be bound by the endless sum of “is it enough?”
lessons.scene: Guiying runs a small breakfast shop in Taichung. Egg and oil prices have both gone up, and this month’s takings are barely better than last month’s. In her accounts book there is a line marked “tithe” that has been empty for two months. After closing today she sits at the till holding an offering envelope, thinking, “Maybe I’ll make it up when business picks up?”
q: Who is God? — God says, “Test me now in this.” What kind of provider is he?
Who am I? — What is your financial life’s boot order right now — God first, or needs first?
How shall I respond? — If you were Guiying, how would you voice your worries to God and take a step of faith?
lessons.jesus: In the temple Jesus watched a poor widow put in two small coins. He said that “she, out of her poverty, gave all that she had to live on” (Mark 12:44). Jesus looked not at the amount but at the order and the trust. He himself went further: he offered not a tenth but the whole of himself. Before his cross, my giving is not a transaction but a response.
lessons.pray: LORD of Armies, you provide everything I have. I confess that I usually count my own needs first and then see what is left for you. Today I want to put you first. When prices rise and income is uncertain, strengthen my faith; and save me from self-righteousness, so that my giving flows from love, not calculation. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Work out a tenth of this month’s income and write it down
If you can’t yet, tell God honestly about your struggle
On payday, set your giving aside first
lessons.noon: “test me now in this” — Lord, right now I give the order back to you and trust you to provide.

lessons.title: A Plan for My Pay
lessons.theme: Diligent planning isn’t unbelief; it is faith put into practice

v: The plans of the diligent surely lead to profit; and everyone who is hasty surely rushes to poverty.
For which of you, desiring to build a tower, doesn’t first sit down and count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it?
Or perhaps, when he has laid a foundation and isn’t able to finish, everyone who sees begins to mock him,
saying, ‘This man began to build and wasn’t able to finish.’

lessons.still: Take a pen and paper and write at the top: “Lord, this salary is yours.” Don’t write any numbers yet. Be still for thirty seconds and ask, “What would you like this month’s money to accomplish for you?”
teach: This week we have seen that the earth is the LORD’s, that we honour him with our wealth, that we are faithful in little things and that God comes first. Today we turn all this into a plan. Proverbs says, “The plans of the diligent surely lead to profit; and everyone who is hasty surely rushes to poverty” (Prov 21:5). Jesus said that anyone building a tower should “first sit down and count the cost”, or people will mock him: “This man began to build and wasn’t able to finish” (Luke 14:28–30). Jesus used the picture to speak of the cost of discipleship, but it also reveals the wisdom of the kingdom: faith never rules out planning. Spiritual people do their sums too.

Walk into a good restaurant kitchen before opening and you will see the chefs doing their prep: onions chopped, sauces made, every ingredient laid out in the order dishes will be served. When the rush comes, the kitchen is busy but calm. A kitchen without prep panics when the orders pile up, and food ends up in the bin. Our pay is the same. Unplanned money feels generous at the start of the month and frantic at the end. Planned money is like a prepped kitchen: every amount is where it should be, ready for the Lord to use.

A simple stewardship plan could have five boxes: giving (God), saving and repaying debt (the future), essentials (family), learning and growth (myself), and generosity (others). The proportions will differ for each person; what matters is the order and the prayer. Among the eight steps of changing our thinking — information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition and multiplication — this is practice: turning this week’s revelation into action. A plan is not about control but about surrender. When Jesus is King, my salary is not just living money; it is funding for his kingdom.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change your thinking and your life will change; change your life and your living will change. This plan is the first step in making “it all belongs to God” real. Building God’s order can begin with my payslip.
lessons.scene: Vivian is a freelance graphic designer in Auckland whose income rises and falls. Last month she landed a big project and immediately bought a new computer and booked flights. This month no work has come in, and the rent is nearly due. She opens a blank spreadsheet; in the first column she writes “Income”, but she has no idea what to put in the second.
q: Who is God? — God is both provider and wise designer. How does he view my planning?
Who am I? — Is your pay more like a prepped kitchen or a kitchen in chaos at rush hour?
How shall I respond? — If you were Vivian, how would you fill in the five boxes of that spreadsheet?
lessons.jesus: Jesus fed five thousand people with five loaves and two fish, and there was more than enough. Yet he told his disciples, “Gather up the broken pieces which are left over, that nothing be lost” (John 6:12). The Lord who multiplies bread also treasures the crumbs. In him abundance and care are not at odds: his generosity never wastes, and his thrift is never stingy.
lessons.pray: Lord who gives wisdom, thank you for entrusting this salary to me. I confess that I often spend on impulse and then panic at the end of the month. Today lead me to write a stewardship plan: let you be in the first box, let my family be cared for, and let me be generous to others. May my plan be not about control, but about surrender. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Allocate this month’s pay into the five boxes
Share your plan with your spouse or a spiritual companion
Set a phone reminder to pray on every payday
lessons.noon: “The plans of the diligent surely lead to profit” — Lord, right now I hand you my plans; be my chief planner.

mem.t: But godliness with contentment is great gain.

lessons.title: Travelling with Hand Luggage
lessons.theme: Godliness with contentment is the real gain

v: But godliness with contentment is great gain.
For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out.
But having food and clothing, we will be content with that.
But those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation, a snare, and many foolish and harmful lusts, such as drown men in ruin and destruction.
For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some have been led astray from the faith in their greed, and have pierced themselves through with many sorrows.

lessons.still: Touch the clothes you are wearing and the lunch you brought, and say to the Lord: “Lord, I have food and clothing; today I will be content with that. Let my heart rest in you, and not be dragged along by wanting more.”
teach: When Paul wrote to young Timothy, some in the Ephesian church supposed “that godliness is a means of gain” (1 Tim 6:5). Paul turned the sum upside down: “But godliness with contentment is great gain” (1 Tim 6:6). The real profit is not the money that godliness might bring, but godliness itself, together with a contented heart. His reason is blunt: “For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out” (1 Tim 6:7). Life is a journey with a start and an end, and the only things we can take with us are our relationship with God and the person we have become in him.

Frequent business travellers know that the passenger with only hand luggage is the freest. No waiting at the baggage carousel, no fear of lost bags, straight from the plane to the meeting. The more luggage, the heavier the journey. When Paul says, “having food and clothing, we will be content with that” (1 Tim 6:8), he is not calling us to a monk’s life of austerity, but inviting us to travel light. Contentment at work does not mean having no ambition to grow; it means refusing to let “more” hijack my time, my family and my conscience.

Paul also warns that “those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation, a snare” (1 Tim 6:9). The problem is not money but desire ruling the heart. The self-centred life imagines that a little more will bring peace, and ends up having “pierced themselves through with many sorrows” (1 Tim 6:10). Contentment is a sign that Jesus is King: when I confess that he is already my greatest treasure, I no longer need a bank balance to prove my worth. Change your thinking, and life becomes lighter, and daily living becomes unhurried.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Shift your perspective — from the temporary to the eternal, from earth to heaven. What you can’t take with you, you needn’t grip so tightly. The self-emptied life is not empty; in Christ it enters into limitless riches.
lessons.scene: Pinyu is a planner at an advertising agency in Taipei. She is well paid, yet it never feels enough. Tonight her colleagues’ group chat is full of designer bags and holiday photos again. She opens a shopping site and puts a bag costing two months’ rent into her basket. Her finger pauses over “Checkout” — and she realises it is the third time this month.
q: Who is God? — Why does God put contentment and godliness together and call it great gain?
Who am I? — What is in your life’s suitcase that you can’t take with you, yet makes the journey heavy?
How shall I respond? — If you were Pinyu, what question would you ask yourself before pressing Checkout?
lessons.jesus: When the disciples worried that Jesus had not eaten, he said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work” (John 4:34). He owned no house and had no savings, yet he was the most satisfied man on earth. His contentment came not from possessions but from his relationship with the Father. Today he invites us to be satisfied from the same source.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that I am often pulled along by wanting more, filling the emptiness inside with shopping, comparison and promotion. Today let me see that you are already my greatest treasure. I have food and clothing; I will be content. Unload the excess baggage of my heart, so that I can follow you travelling light, unhurried and joyful in my work. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Delay one non-essential purchase and decide in seven days
Write down three things of which you can say “I have enough”
While scrolling, stop one comparison and give thanks instead
lessons.noon: “godliness with contentment is great gain” — Lord, right now you are enough for me.

lessons.title: Contentment Is a Learnt Secret
lessons.theme: Contentment isn’t a temperament; it is a lesson learnt in Christ

v: Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learnt in whatever state I am, to be content in it.
I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In any and all circumstances I have learnt the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need.
I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.

lessons.still: Think of the thing that makes you most tense today and hold it in your heart. Say to the Lord: “Lord, whether today goes well or badly, I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.” Breathe slowly three times.
teach: Paul wrote to the Philippians in chains, his future uncertain. The church had sent him a gift, and as he thanked them he said, “I have learnt in whatever state I am, to be content in it” (Phil 4:11). Notice the word “learnt”. Paul was not born content. He had known how to be humbled and how to abound, “both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need”, and in it all he had “learnt the secret” (Phil 4:12). The secret is not a psychological technique but a person: “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me” (Phil 4:13).

Hospital nurses often rotate between day shifts, evenings and nights. New nurses struggle at first — they can’t sleep, can’t eat, and their bodies protest. But an experienced senior nurse finds her rhythm on any shift: she sleeps when it is time to sleep and eats when it is time to eat, and a change of roster doesn’t throw her. She doesn’t have a special constitution; she has learnt. Work has its rosters too: sometimes the “day shift” of pay rises and promotions, sometimes the “night shift” of redundancy and being overlooked. Contentment means learning to find our rhythm in the Lord on every roster.

We often treat Philippians 4:13 as a success slogan, as though leaning on the Lord will win every sale. What Paul means is this: in the Lord I can face lack without despair and plenty without pride. Contentment is not giving up on dreams; it is refusing to let circumstances decide my peace. Lean on the Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head. When the head calculates, it always seems a little short; when the heart looks up, it finds the Lord’s grace already enough.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Our focus is on Jesus, not on circumstances. Among the eight steps of changing our thinking, contentment needs repetition: practising it through good times and hard times until it becomes part of us. Lean with the heart and find joy; lean on the head and find worry.
lessons.scene: Xinyi has been a nurse at a public hospital in Singapore for eight years. This year her department was restructured. She had hoped to become nurse manager, but the post went to a less experienced colleague, and she has been given more night shifts. After handover she sits in the changing room, looking at a message from a classmate about a well-paid job at a private hospital, her heart churning.
q: Who is God? — Paul speaks of “Christ who strengthens me”. Who is this God for you in your lows and your highs?
Who am I? — Which do you find harder for contentment: abundance or need?
How shall I respond? — Does Xinyi need to leave at once, or first to learn contentment? How would you pray with her?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the perfect example of contentment. “Existing in the form of God”, he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil 2:6–7). From heaven’s throne to Bethlehem’s manger, from the crowd’s acclaim to rejection, he remained with the Father in every circumstance. His peace rested not on his surroundings but on his Father, and now he is our strength on every roster.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you came down from heaven’s glory to earthly lowliness, and never complained. I confess that I grow bitter when I miss a promotion, get the shifts I didn’t want, or earn less than others. Teach me the secret of contentment — not by suppressing myself, but by drawing strength from you. Whatever shift I am given today, let me find my rhythm in you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write Philippians 4:13 on a note for today
Thank God for one arrangement you didn’t want
Today, one less complaint and one more encouragement
lessons.noon: “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me” — Lord, right now, whatever my circumstances, I lean on you.

lessons.title: Bigger Barns
lessons.theme: Life isn’t found in abundance but in being rich towards God

v: He said to them, “Beware! Keep yourselves from covetousness, for a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses.”
He spoke a parable to them, saying, “The ground of a certain rich man produced abundantly.
He reasoned within himself, saying, ‘What will I do, because I don’t have room to store my crops?’
He said, ‘This is what I will do. I will pull down my barns, build bigger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods.
I will tell my soul, “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years. Take your ease, eat, drink, and be merry.”’
“But God said to him, ‘You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you. The things which you have prepared—whose will they be?’
So is he who lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich towards God.”
Be free from the love of money, content with such things as you have, for he has said, “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.”

lessons.still: Clench your fists for ten seconds, imagining the things you won’t let go of. Then slowly open them and say: “Lord, I let go of greed. My life doesn’t consist in abundance, for you will never leave me nor forsake me.”
teach: Someone asked Jesus to settle an inheritance dispute. Jesus declined the case and said instead, “Beware! Keep yourselves from covetousness, for a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses” (Luke 12:15). Then he told of a rich man whose land produced abundantly. His first thought: “I will pull down my barns, build bigger ones” (Luke 12:18). From start to finish he talks only to his own soul — no God, no other people. But God said to him, “You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you. The things which you have prepared — whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20). Paul says “the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil” (1 Tim 6:10); this man is its portrait.

Today’s barn might be your phone’s cloud storage. Photos and files pile up, space runs out, and we upgrade the plan: 50GB, then 200GB, then 2TB. Few of us stop to ask whether we really need to keep it all. The rich man’s problem was not that his barns were too small but that he mistook “more” for “safe”. Greed is like a notification that keeps popping up: “Storage almost full.” The more you upgrade, the more often it appears, because the problem was never the capacity.

Hebrews gives the remedy: “Be free from the love of money, content with such things as you have, for he has said, ‘I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you’” (Heb 13:5). The root of greed is often insecurity, and the cure is God’s presence. The self-centred life wants bigger barns for protection, which is really an attempt to replace God. When God is allowed to be God, I can rest in being human. Those who are rich towards God turn their possessions into channels of love rather than bricks for walls.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The rich man had things but no relationships — neither God nor people. Never let things destroy relationships; being rich towards God is the only true wealth.
lessons.scene: Kumar is a senior engineer at a tech company in Kuala Lumpur. The share price has soared and his employee shares have doubled in value. Then a brother from church who runs a small printing business messages him: cash flow is tight, and could Kumar lend him enough to survive three months? On Kumar’s phone two screens are open side by side: his broker’s “Buy more” button, and his brother’s message.
q: Who is God? — God calls the rich man “You foolish one”. How does he judge a life spent storing up treasure for oneself?
Who am I? — Is there a “slightly bigger barn” in your heart that you think would finally make you safe?
How shall I respond? — If you were Kumar, which screen would you answer first? Why?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the one truly rich towards God. He had no land and no barns, yet he kept giving himself away: healing to the sick, forgiveness to sinners, his own body and blood to his disciples. He invites us to make “purses which don’t grow old, a treasure in the heavens that doesn’t fail” (Luke 12:33) — and he himself is that unfailing treasure. In him we need no bigger barns.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess there is a voice in me that wants bigger barns, believing that a little more will make me safe. Forgive my greed and heal my insecurity. You have promised never to leave me nor forsake me; help me trust that word more than my savings. Today make me rich towards you, and open my hands towards others. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Turn off one investing or shopping alert that fuels comparison
Pray for a colleague or church member who is struggling financially
Memorise: “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.”
lessons.noon: “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you” — Lord, right now I trust not in barns but in you.

lessons.title: An Assist Is Ambition Too
lessons.theme: Good ambition seeks God’s glory; bad ambition seeks great things for self

v: Do you seek great things for yourself? Don’t seek them; for, behold, I will bring evil on all flesh,’ says the LORD, ‘but I will let you escape with your life wherever you go.’”
But it shall not be so amongst you, but whoever wants to become great amongst you shall be your servant.
Whoever of you wants to become first amongst you shall be bondservant of all.
For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

lessons.still: Think of the position or achievement you most want, and tell the Lord honestly: “Lord, this is what my heart wants. Purify my motives, so that my ambition is only for your glory.”
teach: Baruch was the scribe of the prophet Jeremiah. Following an unpopular prophet, he had a hard life. Through Jeremiah God said to him, “Do you seek great things for yourself? Don’t seek them” (Jer 45:5). God was not forbidding Baruch to do great things; he was exposing the problem of doing them “for yourself”. Centuries later, James and John came to Jesus: “Grant to us that we may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left hand, in your glory” (Mark 10:37). The other disciples were indignant — perhaps because they hadn’t asked first. Jesus used the moment to redefine greatness: “whoever wants to become great amongst you shall be your servant” (Mark 10:43).

On the football pitch everyone remembers the striker who scores, but people who know the game have deep respect for the player with the most assists. His ambition is not to score himself but for the whole team to win; he passes at the perfect moment to the teammate in the better position. Good ambition is like the assist: I too long for excellence and promotion, because I want my team to be better, more people to benefit, and God’s kingdom to grow where I stand. Bad ambition is the striker who only shoots for himself: his personal stats look great, but the team loses.

Promotion, changing jobs and pay rises are not right or wrong in themselves. The key question is: for whom? Scripture doesn’t tell us to lack drive, but it does tell us to do “nothing through rivalry or through conceit” (Phil 2:3). Pride means leaving my proper place and grasping power; humility means laying down power and returning to my place. Pursue opportunities with humble ambition. If you gain them, they are God’s trust; if you lose them, it is not condemnation. Success is not proof and failure is not judgement. Let Jesus be King, even over your ambitions.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility breeds humility; pride provokes pride. When the disciples competed for the top seats, they ended in indignation and everyone lost. When Jesus became a servant, he created a win–win of serving one another. Good ambition is self-denial: for Jesus, for others, not for myself.
lessons.scene: Boyu is a process engineer at a semiconductor fab in Hsinchu. His manager hints that if he presents this yield improvement as his own initiative, promotion to section head is as good as certain. In fact, half the solution came from a junior colleague who stayed up night after night. Tomorrow he presents to the plant director. He stares at the team list on the final slide, his cursor resting where his junior’s name would go.
q: Who is God? — Jesus said he “came not to be served but to serve”. How does he define true greatness?
Who am I? — Is your ambition more like the assist-maker or the striker who only shoots for himself?
How shall I respond? — If you were Boyu, what would you put on that final slide?
lessons.jesus: Jesus had the greatest purpose of all — to save the world — yet his path was descent. He said, “For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). At the Last Supper he said, “But I am amongst you as one who serves” (Luke 22:27). There was not a trace of self in his purpose; it was all for the Father’s glory and our salvation.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are King of kings, yet you gladly became the servant of all. I confess that I too want the seat on the right or the left; I want credit, position and applause. Purify my motives, so that I pursue excellence to serve others, not to prove myself. In every decision about promotion or a new job, be King, and keep me from seeking great things for myself. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Publicly credit a colleague’s specific contribution today
Write down your career goal, then ask: “For whom?”
Give an opportunity to shine to a colleague who is rarely seen
lessons.noon: “whoever wants to become great amongst you shall be your servant” — Lord, right now I lay down my rivalry and gladly serve.

lessons.title: Turning to the Assets Column
lessons.theme: Gratitude doesn’t ignore what’s lacking; it sees what God has given

v: Praise the LORD, my soul! All that is within me, praise his holy name!
Praise the LORD, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits,
who forgives all your sins, who heals all your diseases,
who redeems your life from destruction, who crowns you with loving kindness and tender mercies,
who satisfies your desire with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.
In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus towards you.

lessons.still: Count five on your fingers. With each one, name a grace you already have today: breath, work, family… Then say quietly, “Praise the LORD, my soul!”
teach: In Psalm 103 David speaks to his own soul: “Praise the LORD, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits” (Ps 103:2). Then he lists them: he forgives all your sins, heals your diseases, redeems your life, crowns you with loving kindness and tender mercies, and satisfies your desire with good things (Ps 103:3–5). David knew flight, betrayal and failure. He gave thanks not because life was easy, but because he deliberately commanded his soul, “don’t forget”, knowing how forgetful the heart can be. Paul says the same: “In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus towards you” (1 Thess 5:18).

Anyone who reads financial statements knows a balance sheet has two sides: liabilities and assets. Anxious people stare only at the liabilities column — mortgage, credit card bills, unmet targets, the promotion that didn’t come. It isn’t that they have no assets; they simply never turn to that column. A gratitude list deliberately turns to the assets: health, family, a colleague’s help, a job that is still there, and the greatest asset of all — forgiveness and eternal life in Christ.

This week we have moved from contentment, to the learnt secret, to refusing greed, to purifying ambition, and now to gratitude. Gratitude is the root of contentment and the antidote to greed. In the eight steps of changing our thinking, this is review and repetition: looking back and counting every day, so that our eyes are re-trained. When I see what I already have, I am no longer ruled by what I lack. Letting Jesus receive all the glory begins with a simple “Thank you, Lord.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Shift your perspective — from what I lack to what God has given. In the 920 life (a self-emptied life bearing the Spirit’s ninefold fruit), the fruits of joy and peace often begin to grow from a gratitude list. Our focus is on Jesus, not on our lack.
lessons.scene: Chunsheng has been a line leader at an electronics factory in Dongguan for twelve years. Orders are down this year, overtime has been cut, and his income has fallen by a third. Back in the dormitory he video-calls his wife in their home town, and she asks about their son’s school fees for next year. After the call he opens the notes app, meaning to work out how much they are short — and sees a message a fellowship brother sent last week: “Why not write a gratitude list?”
q: Who is God? — What do the benefits listed in Psalm 103 show you about the generosity of the Father?
Who am I? — Lately, have you been staring more at life’s liabilities column or its assets column?
How shall I respond? — If you were Chunsheng, which three things would you put on your list? And how would you entrust the school fees to God?
lessons.jesus: At Lazarus’s tomb, with the stone just rolled away and Lazarus not yet out, Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, “Father, I thank you that you listened to me” (John 11:41). His thanksgiving came before the miracle. At the Last Supper he took bread, gave thanks and broke it — the body that would be broken for us. Jesus teaches us that gratitude doesn’t wait for everything to be fine; it says thank you first, in trust.
lessons.pray: Father, my soul will praise you! I confess that I often see only bills, targets and what is missing, and forget all your benefits. Thank you for forgiving me and keeping my life; thank you for today’s work, my family and my companions. When income falls and the way ahead is unclear, help me still to give thanks in everything, trusting you to care for my family. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write ten things you are thankful for in your notes app
Tell a colleague one specific thing you thank them for
Before dinner, share one thanks each with family or flatmates
lessons.noon: “Praise the LORD, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits” — Lord, right now I count your grace.

mem.t: Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.

lessons.title: Not a Service Charge, but a Gift
lessons.theme: God loves not the biggest giver but the cheerful giver

v: Remember this: he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. He who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
And God is able to make all grace abound to you, that you, always having all sufficiency in everything, may abound to every good work.

lessons.still: Place your hand on your chest and feel your heartbeat. Say to the Lord: “Lord, you gave to me freely first. Whatever I give today — time, money or a kind word — let me give it gladly.”
teach: Paul was raising funds for the poor believers in Jerusalem and wrote to the relatively well-off church in Corinth. He didn’t use guilt as pressure. He used a principle every farmer understands: “he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. He who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully” (2 Cor 9:6). Then he said, “Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor 9:7). The Greek word for “cheerful” carries the sense of glad and wholehearted. God cares not only about the amount, but about the look on the giver’s face.

When you eat out, the bill often includes a ten per cent service charge. You pay it whether the service was good or not. But sometimes a waiter’s genuine kindness moves you to leave a tip on top — that is a gift from the heart. A compulsory service charge never makes anyone happy; a voluntary tip leaves you glad. God doesn’t want our giving to become a “heavenly service charge”, as though we lose points if we don’t pay. He invites us to give the way we leave a tip — because his grace has moved us.

How can we give cheerfully? Because “God is able to make all grace abound to you, that you, always having all sufficiency in everything, may abound to every good work” (2 Cor 9:8). The root of cheerfulness is not my abundance but God’s. The self-centred life calculates while giving: if I give, I will have less. The self-emptied life knows: I am simply a transit point for God’s grace, and what comes from him never runs out. Denying ourselves for others is not loss; it lets God’s grace flow through us to many more.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Lean on the Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head. Giving calculated by the head grows tighter with every gift; giving that flows from the heart grows more joyful. Self-denial means for Jesus, for others, not for myself — and joy is its sign.
lessons.scene: Esther teaches at a primary school in Auckland. The school is raising money for a pupil’s family whose house burnt down, and colleagues are passing round a donation envelope in the staffroom. Esther has just paid a large car repair bill and money is tight. Looking at the amounts others have written, a thought pops up: “It’ll look bad if I don’t give.” She holds the pen, unsure what to write.
q: Who is God? — God “is able to make all grace abound to you”. What kind of provider is he?
Who am I? — Was your most recent gift more like paying a service charge or leaving a tip?
How shall I respond? — If you were Esther, what would giving “as he has determined in his heart” and cheerfully look like?
lessons.jesus: A few days before his suffering, a woman broke a jar and poured very costly ointment over Jesus. Some called it a waste, but Jesus said, “She has done what she could” (Mark 14:8). Jesus sees the cheerful heart. He himself is the most cheerful giver of all, “who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame” (Heb 12:2).
lessons.pray: Generous Father, you gave me every good thing first, and did not even hold back your beloved Son. I confess that I often give grudgingly, worrying about what others think and how much I will lose. Renew my heart, so that I give out of gratitude, not pressure. Whether I give much or little today, let there be joy on my face and you in my heart. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before you give anything, pray: “Lord, I give gladly.”
Re-entrust to God one expense you usually resent
Buy a colleague a coffee, expecting nothing back
lessons.noon: “God loves a cheerful giver” — Lord, right now make my heart glad because of you.

lessons.title: Generosity in Deep Poverty
lessons.theme: Generosity doesn’t start with surplus; it starts by giving ourselves to the Lord

v: Moreover, brothers, we make known to you the grace of God which has been given in the assemblies of Macedonia,
how in a severe ordeal of affliction, the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded to the riches of their generosity.
For according to their power, I testify, yes and beyond their power, they gave of their own accord,
begging us with much entreaty to receive this grace and the fellowship in the service to the saints.
This was not as we had expected, but first they gave their own selves to the Lord, and to us through the will of God.

lessons.still: Say quietly: “Lord, before I give anything else, I give myself to you. My time, my abilities and this day are yours first.” Then begin the first task of the day.
teach: Paul introduces the Corinthians to a surprising example: the churches of Macedonia. “In a severe ordeal of affliction, the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded to the riches of their generosity” (2 Cor 8:2). They gave “according to their power … yes and beyond their power”, even “begging us with much entreaty” to share in serving the saints (2 Cor 8:3–4). Paul calls this “the grace of God which has been given in the assemblies of Macedonia” (2 Cor 8:1). Their generosity was not their own achievement; it was grace at work in them.

When the blood donation van parks outside the office, you notice that the queue isn’t made up of the strongest people. One slight accountant comes every three months without fail. “I don’t have much money,” she says, “but I have blood.” Giving blood is unusual: what you give is not an external possession but part of your own body. The Macedonians’ generosity was like that: “first they gave their own selves to the Lord” (2 Cor 8:5). Once people have given themselves to God, giving money, time and skill is simply the natural overflow.

We often say, “When I have more money I’ll give; when I have more time I’ll serve.” The Macedonians proved that the order of generosity is not surplus first, then giving, but self first, then sharing. This is change from the inside out: first life, then relationships, then ministry. Give your life to the Lord first, and generosity grows between people; generous relationships give ministry its life. Letting Jesus be King doesn’t wait for perfect conditions; even in poverty it says, “Lord, I am yours first.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. The Macedonian churches first gave themselves to the Lord (life), then to Paul and his team (relationships), and only then came their rich generosity (ministry). Generosity is the natural fruit of a self-emptied life.
lessons.scene: Jack runs a coffee stall at a hawker centre in Singapore. A company in the nearby office block has moved out, and business has dropped by a fifth. His church has announced an appeal for flood victims in the region, and Jack thinks, “I can barely keep going myself.” As he is closing up, he notices that the elderly cleaner who comes every morning has been ordering only a cup of plain water lately.
q: Who is God? — Paul calls the Macedonians’ generosity “the grace of God”. How does God work in those who are poor?
Who am I? — Do you also say “I’ll give when I have more”? Have you first given yourself to the Lord?
How shall I respond? — If you were Jack, with business down, what could generosity look like right now?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the ultimate generosity in poverty. Straight after the story of the Macedonian churches, Paul writes: “though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich” (2 Cor 8:9). He didn’t give us a little from his surplus; he gave himself completely. We can be generous in our lack because we have first received his boundless grace.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you became poor for me, so that through your poverty I might become rich. I confess that I keep postponing generosity until the day I have more. Today, before I give anything else, I give myself to you. Pour out your grace in my lack, so that like the Macedonian believers I may have abundant joy even in poverty. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: In one sentence of prayer, give yourself to the Lord today
Do one small kindness for someone who has less than you
Set aside a small box in this week’s budget for others
lessons.noon: “their deep poverty abounded to the riches of their generosity” — Lord, right now I give myself to you first.

lessons.title: A Servant on the Treadmill
lessons.theme: Debt brings bondage; the only debt to keep owing is love

v: The rich rule over the poor. The borrower is servant to the lender.
Owe no one anything, except to love one another; for he who loves his neighbour has fulfilled the law.

lessons.still: Take out your wallet or open your credit card app, look at it and say: “Lord, I don’t want to be the lender’s servant; I want to be yours. Give me wisdom and courage to face my accounts honestly.”
teach: Proverbs puts it sharply: “The rich rule over the poor. The borrower is servant to the lender” (Prov 22:7). This is not only moral advice but an observation about life: debt quietly shifts who is in charge of us. In 2 Kings a prophet’s widow was left with her husband’s debts, and the creditor was coming to take her two sons as slaves. Through Elisha God worked a miracle and told her, “Go, sell the oil, and pay your debt” (2 Kgs 4:7). God cares about people trapped in debt, and he leads them out. Paul adds, “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Rom 13:8).

On a gym treadmill you can run until you are drenched in sweat and still be in exactly the same place. High-interest consumer debt is that treadmill. You make your payments every month, but the interest means the balance barely moves; your salary is swallowed by instalments as soon as it arrives. You run harder and harder and get nowhere. Worse, the speed is not set by you but by the lender. That is exactly what “the borrower is servant to the lender” means.

Scripture does not say all borrowing is sin. A mortgage or sensible business borrowing can be used with wisdom and integrity. But it warns us not to let debt become our master. If credit card debt or loan sharks are crushing you, the first step is not shame but honesty; where needed, seek out someone you trust or professional debt advice. Letting Jesus be King includes letting him be Lord of my bank account, and the only debt I should keep owing is the debt of love.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility means laying down power and returning to my proper place. Borrowing for image or pleasure is trying to live above my place; returning to it and living within my means brings freedom in the Lord. Never let things destroy relationships, and never sell your freedom for things.
lessons.scene: Hongzhi is in his second year out of university, working as a software tester in Taipei. He bought a new phone and laptop on credit card instalments, and took out a personal loan to attend a friend’s wedding overseas. This month, once the instalments are deducted, he has NT$8,000 left to last until payday. Then a text arrives from his bank: “You have a cash advance limit available for immediate use.”
q: Who is God? — God helped an indebted widow through Elisha. How does he view people trapped in debt?
Who am I? — Is there a debt in your life that makes you feel like you’re on a treadmill?
How shall I respond? — If you were Hongzhi, facing that text, what step could you take today?
lessons.jesus: We all owed God a debt we could never repay. In Jesus’ parable, the master, “being moved with compassion, released him and forgave him the debt” (Matt 18:27). On the cross Jesus wiped out “the handwriting in ordinances which was against us”, “nailing it to the cross” (Col 2:14). He paid our debt of sin in full, so that from now on we owe only one thing: to love one another.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for cancelling on the cross the debt I could never pay. I confess that I have sometimes let debt rule me for the sake of image or pleasure. Give me courage to face my accounts, wisdom to live within my means, and humility to ask for help. Let me be your servant, not the lender’s, and let me spend my life owing the debt of love. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: List all your debts and interest rates, and give them to the Lord
Cancel one unnecessary instalment plan or subscription
If your debt is heavy, arrange to talk with someone you trust
lessons.noon: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” — Lord, right now I want to owe only the debt of love.

lessons.title: More Blessed to Give
lessons.theme: Those who give taste the blessing promised by the Lord Jesus himself

v: I coveted no one’s silver, gold, or clothing.
You yourselves know that these hands served my necessities, and those who were with me.
In all things I gave you an example, that so labouring you ought to help the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”

lessons.still: Open your hands, palms up, and say: “Lord, first I receive from you.” Then turn your palms down: “Now I will share what you have given me with the people I meet today.”
teach: At Miletus Paul said farewell to the elders of Ephesus. It was a tearful parting (Acts 20:37–38). Looking back on his ministry he said, “I coveted no one’s silver, gold, or clothing. You yourselves know that these hands served my necessities, and those who were with me” (Acts 20:33–34). Paul was a tentmaker by trade (Acts 18:3) and used his craft to support himself and his co-workers. As he left, he quoted a saying of the Lord Jesus recorded nowhere in the Gospels, yet precious beyond measure: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35).

The software world has an open-source culture: developers publish their code for anyone in the world to use and improve for free. On the surface they are giving away their hard work. Yet precisely because of this the whole ecosystem grows richer, they benefit from others’ contributions, and they gain a satisfaction no salary can measure. Givers don’t become poorer; they enter a larger cycle. As Proverbs says, “He who waters shall be watered also himself” (Prov 11:25).

Paul says giving is so that we “help the weak” (Acts 20:35). At work, giving is not only donating money. It is passing on experience to new staff, giving time to a colleague who needs company, and sharing credit with the team. The self-centred life only wants to receive: pay, recognition, service. The self-emptied life learns to give, because it knows everything was a free gift from God. Jesus said, “Freely you received, so freely give” (Matt 10:8). Those who live this way taste the blessing the Lord himself promised.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The “3” in 235 is the relationship of spiritual parents and children. “More blessed to give” means pouring what we have received into the next generation. Paul set an example with his own hands; Jesus is my example, and I become an example for others.
lessons.scene: Xiaoyan is the HR manager at a multinational company in Shanghai. Over ten years she has developed a practical approach to recruitment interviews. Her two new HR officers keep getting stuck, and a colleague warns her, “Don’t teach them too much — train your apprentice and you’ll starve yourself.” This afternoon one of the officers knocks on her door and asks timidly, “Xiaoyan, could you look over my interview questions?”
q: Who is God? — Jesus said, “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” What does that show you about God’s own heart?
Who am I? — At work, are you more used to receiving or giving? What is in your hands that you could give away?
How shall I respond? — If you were Xiaoyan, how would you answer that knock on the door?
lessons.jesus: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” are Jesus’ own words, and a portrait of his whole life. He healed, taught and fed the crowds, and in the end gave his very life. With his hands he washed his disciples’ feet, and he let those same hands be nailed to the cross. What he gave we can never repay; we can give only because we have first received everything from him.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you said it is more blessed to give than to receive, and you are the greatest giver of all. I confess that I fear giving will leave me with less, and that teaching others will make me less valuable. Remove the sense of scarcity in my heart, so that I gladly share my experience, time and resources with those in need. Today let me taste the blessing you promised. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Teach a colleague one skill you know well
Share a useful work template with your team
Say “Let me help you” at least once today
lessons.noon: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” — Lord, right now I gladly share what you have given me.

lessons.title: Don’t Hit Snooze
lessons.theme: Generosity isn’t just a kind thought; it is doing it today

v: Don’t withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in the power of your hand to do it.
Don’t say to your neighbour, “Go, and come again; tomorrow I will give it to you,” when you have it by you.
Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.
So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good towards all men, and especially towards those who are of the household of the faith.

lessons.still: Think of someone you’ve wanted to help but keep putting off. Say their name in your heart and tell the Lord, “Lord, let me act today, and not say to them, ‘Come again tomorrow.’”
teach: Proverbs says, “Don’t withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in the power of your hand to do it. Don’t say to your neighbour, ‘Go, and come again; tomorrow I will give it to you,’ when you have it by you” (Prov 3:27–28). The wise know that kindness’s greatest enemy is not refusal but delay. Paul encourages us too: “Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up. So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good towards all men” (Gal 6:9–10). Opportunities have an expiry date; once gone, they don’t return.

Every alarm clock and to-do app has a “Snooze” button. Pressing it once is handy, twice does no harm, but many things quietly expire through one snooze after another — the call you meant to make, the thank-you card you meant to write, the gift you meant to give. In the parable of the Good Samaritan, perhaps the priest and the Levite both had their reasons for “later”. Only the Samaritan stopped there and then, bandaged the wounds, set the man on his animal and paid the innkeeper. Generosity often needs just this: don’t hit snooze.

This week we have learnt about cheerful giving, generosity in poverty, freedom from debt and the blessing of giving. Today we turn it into one concrete action: a gift, a meal, an introduction for a friend who has lost their job, a weekend spent with an elderly neighbour who lives alone. In the eight steps of changing our thinking, this is practice — and the beginning of multiplication, because one person’s generosity so often sparks another’s.
lessons.light: 321 Light: In 920, everyone connected to me is my “2”. This month’s act of generosity is living out the self-emptied “0” towards one of my “2”s, and bearing the “9” — the fruit of goodness and kindness. Humility breeds humility, and generosity breeds generosity.
lessons.scene: Guanting is a case officer at a district office in Kaohsiung. The office cleaner has been taking a lot of leave lately; he hears her grandson is in hospital and the medical bills are heavy. Several times he has meant to help, but felt awkward and thought, “I’ll wait until the year-end bonus comes.” Just before leaving today, he sees her alone in the pantry, quietly counting loose change.
q: Who is God? — God says “we will reap in due season”. How does he view our seemingly small acts of kindness?
Who am I? — Is there a good deed in your heart that you’ve snoozed several times?
How shall I respond? — If you were Guanting, walking into the pantry now, how would you speak so as not to embarrass her?
lessons.jesus: Jesus never hit snooze. When a blind man cried out by the roadside, he stopped. When a widow’s funeral procession passed, he went over to comfort her. When Lazarus fell ill, he went to Bethany despite the danger. He didn’t wait for us to improve before dying for us: “while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Rom 5:8).
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you never say to me, “Come again tomorrow.” I confess that I keep good intentions in my heart and put them off again and again. Today open my eyes to the needs around me, give me courage to act now, and give me wisdom to give thoughtfully, without embarrassing anyone. May there be one concrete act of generosity this month, because you are my King. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Put this month’s act of generosity and its date in your calendar
Make that caring phone call you’ve been putting off — today
Ask a companion to check next month: “Did you do it?”
lessons.noon: “as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good towards all men” — Lord, right now I won’t delay; I will act.

mem.t: The integrity of the upright shall guide them, but the perverseness of the treacherous shall destroy them.

lessons.title: That Little Bit on the Scales
lessons.theme: The fairness God cares about hides in every tiny mark on the scale

v: A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but accurate weights are his delight.
“‘You shall do no unrighteousness in judgement, in measures of length, of weight, or of quantity.
You shall have just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin. I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.

lessons.still: Picture a pair of scales in front of you, perfectly balanced. Say to the Lord: “Lord, every price I quote, every quantity I measure and every figure I write today will be placed on your scales. Make me fair, for you are a righteous God.”
teach: Ancient markets had no digital scales; every trade relied on a balance and weights. A dishonest merchant kept two sets of weights in his bag: heavy ones for buying, light ones for selling. Each deal was out by only a little, but over time it added up. Proverbs says, “A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but accurate weights are his delight” (Prov 11:1). “Abomination” is a strong word, often used in the Old Testament for idolatry. In the law God had commanded, “You shall have just balances, just weights”, and immediately added, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Lev 19:36). Fairness is the way of life of a redeemed people.

Few of us use a balance today, but every industry has its scales. A food packet labelled 500 grams actually holds 480; a timesheet says eight hours, though one was spent scrolling; a quotation pads the costs; an inspection report skips a test. Every figure is a weight, and no one can see that little bit of difference. But God sees. To God, the scales are not just a tool; they are a picture of a person’s heart at work.

Why does God care so much about “a little bit”? Because behind a false balance lies a heart that wants a little more and wants to be its own master — the self-centred life. Accurate weights declare: I trust God as my provider; I don’t need to cut corners to secure myself. Letting Jesus be King means making his righteousness the standard for every mark on my scale. Change your thinking and your living will change: when I am honest down to the decimal point, God’s kingdom is revealed at my workbench.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Bible is my standard. Accurate weights delight God, and they are the foundation stone of building God’s order — the trust of a team or a company rests on the scales in each person’s hands.
lessons.scene: Yafen is a quality control supervisor at a food factory in Tainan. Every packet in this batch of meat floss is about five grams short, beyond the tolerance allowed for the label. The factory manager says, “It’s only a little. Repacking will take another day and we’ll miss the delivery.” The dispatch note is on her desk awaiting her signature, and the lorry is already waiting outside the window.
q: Who is God? — God says accurate weights are his delight. What kind of details does this God care about?
Who am I? — What are the “scales” in your work? Have you ever tampered with them, even a little?
How shall I respond? — If you were Yafen, before you sign, how could you hold to honesty while still respecting the manager?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the one who did not sin, and in whose mouth no deceit was found (1 Pet 2:22). He never gave short measure — he never discounted the truth, and never gave love by the short weight. At the cross God’s just scales were not tilted: the penalty for sin fell fully on him, so that we who had cheated might be declared righteous through him.
lessons.pray: Righteous Lord, your scales never tilt. I confess that I have sometimes reported a little more and worked a little less, thinking no one would know. Forgive me and cleanse my hands. Today, in every quote, every shipment and every form, keep me honest and without deceit, because I trust you as my provider. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Check one set of figures you handle today for accuracy
Fill in your timesheet truthfully, down to fifteen minutes
Identify the “scales” in your work and pray over them
lessons.noon: “accurate weights are his delight” — Lord, right now let every figure in my hands be fair.

lessons.title: An Offering with a Filter
lessons.theme: One small lie can cost a great deal before God

v: But a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a possession,
and kept back part of the price, his wife also being aware of it, then brought a certain part and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
But Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back part of the price of the land?
While you kept it, didn’t it remain your own? After it was sold, wasn’t it in your power? How is it that you have conceived this thing in your heart? You haven’t lied to men, but to God.”
Ananias, hearing these words, fell down and died. Great fear came on all who heard these things.

lessons.still: Pick up your phone and glance at your profile photo, then put it down and say to the Lord: “Lord, I don’t want to live behind a filter. Today, before you and before others, I just want to be real.”
teach: In the early church believers shared everything. Barnabas sold a field and laid the money at the apostles’ feet (Acts 4:36–37). Ananias and Sapphira also sold property, but “kept back part of the price” and laid the rest at the apostles’ feet (Acts 5:2). Peter made it clear: before it was sold it was theirs, and after the sale the money was in their power (Acts 5:4). Their sin was not giving less but pretending to give everything: “You haven’t lied to men, but to God” (Acts 5:4). The outcome is shocking: Ananias “fell down and died”. In the church’s infancy God used this solemn judgement to protect the truthfulness of his people.

Beauty filters on social media can smooth your skin and enlarge your eyes in an instant. Using one now and then does no harm, but if every photo is edited, eventually we become afraid to be seen as we really are. Ananias and Sapphira put a filter on their offering: they wanted a reputation for generosity without paying its price. Work has plenty of filters too: presenting the team’s results as my own, dressing up a delay as the client’s fault, turning “I forgot” into “there was a system error”.

“Why has Satan filled your heart to lie?” (Acts 5:3). Lies often begin with a desire to be thought well of. The self-centred life fears that the real me isn’t good enough and adds points with a lie — but every lie needs another to hold it up. God may not judge immediately today, but lies still corrode trust, relationships and conscience. The good news is that we can take the filter off: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility means laying down power and returning to my proper place. Ananias wanted a reputation that wasn’t his — leaving his place. Honestly admitting my limits is returning to my place: letting people be people, and letting God be God.
lessons.scene: Desmond is a property agent in Singapore. The owner has told him privately that the bathroom in this flat had a leak repaired last year, and asked him “not to bring it up”. Today a young couple are viewing. The wife points to a freshly painted patch on the bathroom ceiling and asks, “Was there a problem here before?” The owner is standing right beside them, looking at Desmond.
q: Who is God? — Peter says, “You haven’t lied to men, but to God.” What does this show you about how God sees lies?
Who am I? — What “filters” do you use at work? What are you most afraid of people seeing?
How shall I respond? — If you were Desmond, how would you answer the wife right now?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). He never put a filter on himself: misunderstood, he didn’t rush to defend himself; praised, he didn’t puff up. Before Pilate he said, “For this reason I have been born, and for this reason I have come into the world, that I should testify to the truth” (John 18:37). He died for people like us who love our image and tell lies, so that in his grace we no longer need to pretend.
lessons.pray: Lord of truth, I confess that I often use filters: exaggerating results, covering mistakes, telling little lies to smooth things over. Forgive me, and give me courage to live in the truth. Today, before clients, before my manager and on social media, let me speak the truth even when it costs me. I trust that your grace is enough for me. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Tell no smoothing-over white lies today
Own up to someone about a mistake you once covered
Name one “filter” you often use and give it to the Lord
lessons.noon: “You haven’t lied to men, but to God” — Lord, right now I want to be honest before you, without pretence.

lessons.title: Zacchaeus’s Product Recall
lessons.theme: True repentance leads to concrete restitution and repair

v: When Jesus came to the place, he looked up and saw him, and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.”
He hurried, came down, and received him joyfully.
When they saw it, they all murmured, saying, “He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner.”
Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.”
Jesus said to him, “Today, salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham.
For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.”

lessons.still: Think of someone you have wronged, and honestly speak their name to the Lord. Then say: “Lord, you accepted me first. Give me courage to repair what I can.”
teach: Zacchaeus was Jericho’s “chief tax collector, and he was rich” (Luke 19:2), his wealth very likely built on extortion. As Jesus passed by, he looked up at him in the tree and said, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house” (Luke 19:5). The crowd muttered, but Jesus accepted him first. Then Zacchaeus stood and said, “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much” (Luke 19:8). The law’s heaviest penalties for theft were “five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep” (Exod 22:1); Zacchaeus chose a very high standard of his own accord. Jesus declared, “Today, salvation has come to this house” (Luke 19:9).

When a responsible car maker discovers a faulty part in a batch of vehicles, it issues a recall: it contacts every owner, replaces the part for free and even compensates for losses. It is costly and embarrassing, yet it wins back customers’ trust. Zacchaeus’s fourfold restitution was a “life recall notice”. He didn’t just say sorry in his heart; he went to find people and repay them, one account at a time. True repentance is not only a feeling but an action.

Notice the order: Zacchaeus did not repay first so that Jesus would accept him; Jesus accepted him first, and then Zacchaeus turned around. Grace comes first and change follows — that is the order of the gospel. Change your thinking and your life changes; change your life and your living changes. Zacchaeus’s attitude to money was overturned over a single meal. You too may have something to “recall”: an inflated claim, credit taken from someone else, a word that wounded a colleague. Where needed, ask a pastor or someone you trust how best to put it right. Repair does not earn salvation; it flows from salvation already come.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Zacchaeus turned from loving money to loving people, using money to repair the relationships he had damaged. Change in thinking, life, living and relationships was visible in him within a single day.
lessons.scene: Zhenbang runs a used car dealership in Penang. More than ten years ago, when the business was just starting, he wound back the mileage on several cars before selling them. Last month he was baptised, and this week the pastor preached on Zacchaeus; he couldn’t sleep all night. Today he digs out his old ledger and looks at the names of several former customers whose phone numbers he still has, his finger resting on the first number.
q: Who is God? — Jesus first said to Zacchaeus, “today I must stay at your house.” What kind of grace does that show you?
Who am I? — Is there something in your life that needs a “recall”?
How shall I respond? — If you were Zhenbang, how would you prepare yourself before making that call?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19:10). He didn’t wait for Zacchaeus to improve; he looked up at him first, called his name and entered his home. Later he paid a far higher price than fourfold for Zacchaeus and for us — his own life. His recall is total: there is no lost person he is unwilling to bring back.
lessons.pray: Lord who seeks the lost, thank you for calling my name first and entering my life. I confess that I too have wronged people: things I took, credit I seized, words that hurt. Give me Zacchaeus’s courage, not only to regret in my heart but to make concrete repair. Show me whom to approach and how, and give me wisdom and humility. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down one wrong you need to put right
Pray today for the person you wronged
Ask a pastor or spiritual companion how best to make amends
lessons.noon: “Today, salvation has come to this house” — Lord, right now, by your grace, I am ready to turn around.

lessons.title: The Steel You Can’t See
lessons.theme: Honesty lives in the details of reports, expense claims and CVs

v: We are avoiding this, that any man should blame us concerning this abundance which is administered by us.
Having regard for honourable things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men.
Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who do the truth are his delight.

lessons.still: Open the first document or report you need to submit today. Don’t send it yet. Say to the Lord: “Lord, every word here is before you. Make me honest in the details too.”
teach: When Paul raised money for Jerusalem, he arranged for trustworthy brothers to travel with him and handle the gift. He said, “We are avoiding this, that any man should blame us concerning this abundance which is administered by us. Having regard for honourable things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men” (2 Cor 8:20–21). Paul wasn’t content with a clear conscience; he set up a transparent arrangement so that others could see. Proverbs agrees: “Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who do the truth are his delight” (Prov 12:22).

The most important part of a building is often the steel reinforcement you never see. The façade can be beautifully clad and the lobby impressively fitted out, but if the rebar is skimped, the truth comes out the moment an earthquake strikes. At work the steel is the details nobody examines closely: a figure in a report, a receipt on an expense claim, a line on a CV. Exaggerate a little, adjust a little, pad a little, and normally no one notices. But an earthquake of trust will come one day.

Honesty is not just not lying; like Paul, it is “having regard for honourable things” — actively making things transparent. Keep complete receipts, add notes to your reports, write your CV truthfully, and say so when you don’t know something. If a manager asks you to falsify accounts or break the law, obedience has limits: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29); where needed, seek out someone you trust or professional help. Letting Jesus be King means letting him be the final reviewer of every document I produce.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Building God’s order is not only personal honesty; like Paul, it means designing transparent systems. Change your thinking and your living will change: when I treat every document as something presented to God, the details become worship.
lessons.scene: Shuzhen has been the accountant at a small company in Taipei for ten years. The company is applying for a bank loan, and the boss calls her into his office: “Push last year’s revenue up by twenty per cent. I have contacts at the bank. You’ve been with me long enough — you understand, don’t you?” Shuzhen knows the company really does need the money, and the boss has always treated her well.
q: Who is God? — God says “those who do the truth are his delight”. Does he care about the details no one sees?
Who am I? — What is the hidden “steel” in your work? Has any of it been skimped?
How shall I respond? — If you were Shuzhen, how would you answer your boss, holding to honesty while keeping your respect for him?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). His truth is not harsh, and his grace is not without principle. His whole life withstood the strictest scrutiny; even Pilate, who interrogated him, said, “I find no basis for a charge against him” (John 18:38). This sinless Lord bore judgement for us who have failed in the details, and now he sets new steel of honesty within us.
lessons.pray: Lord of truth, you delight in those who do the truth. I confess that I have polished reports, blurred expense claims and exaggerated my CV. Forgive me and strengthen the steel of my life. If anyone asks me to do something dishonest today, give me courage to say no, and the wisdom and gentleness to say it respectfully. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Check today’s report: every figure must have a basis
Review your CV and remove any exaggeration
Complete the receipts for one claim so it can stand an audit
lessons.noon: “those who do the truth are his delight” — Lord, right now let me please you in the details no one sees.

lessons.title: Flying by Instruments
lessons.theme: The upright don’t navigate by feelings; integrity guides them

v: The integrity of the upright shall guide them, but the perverseness of the treacherous shall destroy them.
Riches don’t profit in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death.
The righteousness of the blameless will direct his way, but the wicked shall fall by his own wickedness.
The righteousness of the upright shall deliver them, but the unfaithful will be trapped by evil desires.

Then the presidents and the local governors sought to find occasion against Daniel as touching the kingdom; but they could find no occasion or fault, because he was faithful. There wasn’t any error or fault found in him.

lessons.still: Close your eyes and imagine yourself in thick fog. Say to the Lord: “Lord, today when I can’t see the way ahead, let your word be my instruments and your integrity guide me.”
teach: Proverbs says, “The integrity of the upright shall guide them, but the perverseness of the treacherous shall destroy them” (Prov 11:3). Integrity carries the sense of wholeness — being the same inside and out. The upright don’t need to recalculate the costs and benefits every time; their integrity is itself their direction. Daniel was such a man. He served as a senior official in a foreign court, and his envious colleagues searched for something to use against him, “but they could find no occasion or fault, because he was faithful. There wasn’t any error or fault found in him” (Dan 6:4). In the end they could only attack his faith.

Pilots flying in cloud can suffer spatial disorientation: the body feels the aircraft is level when it is actually banking and descending. So they are trained not to trust their feelings but to trust their instruments. Work has plenty of cloud — sales pressure, a manager’s hints, colleagues egging you on, “everyone does it”. In the cloud, feelings deceive, and “just this once” feels like level flight. Integrity is our instrument panel: God’s word and a heart that is the same inside and out still point the true direction when we can’t see.

This week we have looked at honest scales, Ananias’s filter, Zacchaeus’s recall and the hidden steel. All of it comes down to one word: integrity. Integrity is not perfection but consistency — the same person before God, before others and where no one is watching. This is the self-emptied life: no longer twisting the truth for my own interests, because “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal 2:20). Those who let Jesus be King will in the end be guided home by their integrity.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Holy Spirit is my guide. In the fog of work, lean on the Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head. People of integrity keep their focus on Jesus, not on circumstances — and such a life becomes an instrument panel for others too.
lessons.scene: After graduating, Ziyang became a medical sales representative for a pharmaceutical company in Chengdu, under heavy sales pressure. His supervisor coaches him: “Give the doctors a red envelope every month and the prescriptions will go up. Everyone does it.” The month is nearly over and he has reached only sixty per cent of his target. Tonight he stands in the hospital car park, holding a stack of envelopes his supervisor pressed into his hands.
q: Who is God? — God says the integrity of the upright will guide them. How does he lead people through the fog?
Who am I? — When your feelings and the truth disagree, which do you usually trust?
How shall I respond? — If you were Ziyang, what would you do with those envelopes? Besides praying, whom could he talk to?
lessons.jesus: After fasting forty days and nights in the wilderness, Jesus was tempted; three times the devil offered him shortcuts that looked reasonable. Each time he answered, “It is written” (Matt 4:4–10), letting God’s word be his instruments. His whole life was consistent inside and out, and he did not swerve even at the cross. Now his integrity lives in us by the Holy Spirit, guiding us on the upright path.
lessons.pray: Upright Lord, let your word be my instruments and your integrity guide me. I confess that under pressure and in the fog I often trust my feelings, thinking “just this once” doesn’t matter. Make me the same inside and out, the same person in public and in private. If anyone urges me to take a shortcut, give me courage and wisdom, and provide companions I can talk to. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Put Proverbs 11:3 on your phone wallpaper or a note
Find a companion to pray with about one “everyone does it” pressure
In one small matter today, be the same in public and private
lessons.noon: “The integrity of the upright shall guide them” — Lord, right now, in the fog, I will trust your instruments.

mem.t: But Peter and the apostles answered, We must obey God rather than men.

lessons.title: God Rather Than Men
lessons.theme: When an order collides with God's word, stay loyal to the highest Lord

v: When they had brought them, they set them before the council. The high priest questioned them,
saying, “Didn’t we strictly command you not to teach in this name? Behold, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and intend to bring this man’s blood on us.”
But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than men.
The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you killed, hanging him on a tree.
God exalted him with his right hand to be a Prince and a Saviour, to give repentance to Israel, and remission of sins.
We are his witnesses of these things; and so also is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.”

lessons.still: Before work, rest your open hands on your knees for thirty seconds. Say to the Lord: “Lord, today many voices will tell me what to do, but you are the highest. Help me hear you above them all.”
teach: The apostles had just been jailed, released by an angel, and were back in the temple teaching at dawn. The high priest demanded, “Didn’t we strictly command you not to teach in this name?” Peter’s answer was one sentence: “We must obey God rather than men.” Notice what he did not do. He did not shout or stir up a crowd to overthrow the council. Standing before his judges, he calmly stated his priorities and then preached Jesus — the one hung on a tree, whom God exalted “to be a Prince and a Saviour”.

Every workplace has an organisation chart: team leader, manager, director, board. Most of the time, honouring that chart is honouring God, because God establishes authority. But at the very top of the chart is a box we often forget: the Lord Jesus. Just as a company policy cannot override the law of the land, no manager’s instruction can override the word of God. When the two collide, you are not being uncooperative; you are simply following the real chain of command.

This is not a licence to rebel. Peter could say “obey God” because he obeyed God every day — even after a flogging he left “rejoicing” (Acts 5:41). True refusal grows out of humility, not pride: I am not trying to be king; I am letting Jesus be King. So ask first: does God’s word clearly forbid this, or do I simply dislike it? Is this a line of conscience or a line of ego? Once you know, stand firm, gently. And where needed, talk it through with a trusted spiritual elder or a qualified professional.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility means laying down power and returning to my proper place. Obeying God is not grabbing control; it is handing the final say back to him and letting Jesus be King. Scripture is my standard — what makes me say no is not my mood but God’s word.
lessons.scene: Yuting sells medical devices. Just before quarter end, her manager asks her to fill in visit records for several clinics she never actually visited, so the team can hit target and everyone gets a bonus. He pats her shoulder: “Everyone does it. Nobody gets hurt.” She opens her tablet, and the cursor blinks in the “Visit date” box.
q: Who is God? — Peter says God made Jesus “a Prince and a Saviour”. What authority does this King have over your work today?
Who am I? — Are you more likely to go along out of fear of people, or to refuse out of pride?
