How shall I respond? — If you were Yuting, how could you refuse to falsify records while still respecting your manager and offering another way forward?
lessons.jesus: Before Pilate, Jesus neither fought nor flattered. He said, “You would have no power at all against me, unless it were given to you from above” (John 19:11). He obeyed the Father all the way to the cross — and because he obeyed God perfectly, we receive forgiveness and the courage to stand before people.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are my highest Lord. If anyone asks me today to do what grieves you, give me clear discernment, a gentle tongue and a steady heart. Keep me from dressing up my impatience as a conviction. Be King over my visit records, my reports and every signature I sign. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down one ‘grey’ issue at work this week
Pray for your line manager for one minute
Prepare a line: “I want us to hit target, but I can’t do this one”
lessons.noon: “We must obey God rather than men.” — Lord, right now I hand every signature over to you.

lessons.title: The Midwives’ Courage
lessons.theme: Those who fear God protect life, even under a king’s command

v: The king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives, of whom the name of the one was Shiphrah, and the name of the other Puah,
and he said, “When you perform the duty of a midwife to the Hebrew women, and see them on the birth stool, if it is a son, then you shall kill him; but if it is a daughter, then she shall live.”
But the midwives feared God, and didn’t do what the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the baby boys alive.
The king of Egypt called for the midwives, and said to them, “Why have you done this thing and saved the boys alive?”
The midwives said to Pharaoh, “Because the Hebrew women aren’t like the Egyptian women; for they are vigourous and give birth before the midwife comes to them.”
God dealt well with the midwives, and the people multiplied, and grew very mighty.
Because the midwives feared God, he gave them families.

lessons.still: Place your hand on your chest and feel your heartbeat for thirty seconds. Pray: “Lord, you are the Lord of life. Every person who passes through my hands today is someone you love. Teach me to fear you more than I fear anyone.”
teach: Pharaoh was the most powerful man in the world, and he gave two Hebrew midwives an order: kill every baby boy at birth. Scripture records their names — Shiphrah and Puah — yet never tells us this Pharaoh’s name. They did not march or publish a statement. In the birthing room they quietly did one thing: they “saved the baby boys alive”. And the reason is given plainly: “the midwives feared God”.

Interpreters differ on whether the midwives’ reply to Pharaoh was wholly truthful; Scripture does not praise their explanation. It says God dealt well with them “because the midwives feared God”. The point is not their cleverness but the scales in their hearts. Each of us carries an invisible set of scales at work: on one side the boss, the appraisal, the pay cheque; on the other, God. To fear God is to let his side always weigh more, even when the weights on the other side look terrifying.

Fearing God is not living in dread. It is living in the security of being seen. People see only the spreadsheet; God sees the hands in the birthing room that refused to harm. Change your thinking and you change your life: when I move from “afraid of my manager’s anger” to “longing to please the Lord”, I am no longer pushed around by every order. And God did not forget them — “he gave them families”. Faithfulness may not bring promotion, but it always brings God’s presence and remembrance.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Shift your perspective — from the human to the divine, from the temporary to the eternal. Pharaoh’s decree seemed to decide everything, but God is the one who keeps the names. People matter more than tasks: no performance target is worth a single life.
lessons.scene: Suzhen is the head nurse at a residential care home. To cut costs, management wants her to reduce the night shift from three staff to two, while still reporting “three” at inspection. She knows several residents could fall at any moment during the night. The director says, “If you won’t sign, I’ll find someone who will.” She holds the roster and cannot bring herself to sign.
q: Who is God? — God dealt well with the midwives. What does that show you about what God values?
Who am I? — In your work, who are the vulnerable ones you are called to ‘save alive’?
How shall I respond? — How can Suzhen protect the residents and raise her concerns through proper channels? Who could she turn to for help?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was born, he too met a king who killed baby boys — Herod — yet God protected him. Later he said, “I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly” (John 10:10). He is the Good Shepherd who truly laid down his life for the weak, and his reverent obedience took him all the way to the cross.
lessons.pray: Lord of life, thank you for seeing every person at work who could easily be sacrificed. Give me the midwives’ courage to fear you more than my managers, and the wisdom to protect people in the right way. When I am afraid of losing my job, remind me that you deal well with those who fear you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Check in on the most overlooked person at work
Pray before replying to an unreasonable request
Write: “I fear God more than I fear ___”
lessons.noon: “But the midwives feared God” — Lord, right now I too choose to fear you more than people.

lessons.title: A Clear Conscience
lessons.theme: Keep a conscience void of offence towards God and people

v: In this I also practise always having a conscience void of offence towards God and men.
holding faith and a good conscience, which some having thrust away made a shipwreck concerning the faith,

lessons.still: Close your eyes. Like clearing notifications on your phone, hand over to the Lord, one by one, the things still ‘lit up’ in your heart. Pray: “Lord, if anything troubles my conscience, shine your light on it; if I have already confessed it, help me let it go.”
teach: Paul stood trial before Governor Felix, accused of stirring up unrest. He did not rush to counter-attack. He simply stated the principle of his life: “I also practise always having a conscience void of offence towards God and men.” Practise — a clear conscience is not something we are born with; it is trained day by day. Writing to Timothy, Paul warned that some, having thrust a good conscience away, “made a shipwreck concerning the faith”.

Your conscience is like the warning light on a car’s dashboard. When it comes on, you can pull over and check, or you can stick a bit of tape over it and keep driving. Most workplace shipwrecks do not happen overnight. They start with one small piece of tape: a padded expense claim, a “ship it and we’ll test later” release, a casual “the client will never notice”. In time the light stops coming on — not because the car is fine, but because we no longer look.

The good news is that a conscience can be restored. The blood of Christ cleanses our conscience so we need not carry guilt into the office (see Hebrews 9:14). A clear conscience does not mean never failing; it means returning to God at once to confess, and putting things right with people where needed. This is ‘review and correction’ from the eight steps: letting the Holy Spirit run a dashboard check each day, so we can lift our heads before God and people alike.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Holy Spirit is my guide. To rely on the Spirit with my heart is to refuse to tape over the warning light. Change works from the inside out: first a clean conscience, then relationships and ministry can stand firm.
lessons.scene: Shijie is a software engineer at a start-up. Tomorrow the product launches publicly, but he has found a flaw that could leak some users’ data. The product manager says, “Ship now, patch it next version. If we delay, the investors will walk.” He stares at the red line on his screen, his finger hovering over “Deploy”.
q: Who is God? — Why does God care that our conscience is clear “towards God and men” — both?
Who am I? — Has there been anywhere lately where you’ve taped over your conscience’s warning light?
How shall I respond? — How can Shijie honestly report the risk and offer a workable plan, rather than just saying “No”?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the only person who never once wronged his conscience; even those who sought false witness against him “found none” (Matthew 26:60). Yet he carried every accusation for us whose consciences are stained. His blood washes us, so we do not live by pretending to be spotless, but stand in his righteousness.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that your precious blood cleanses my conscience. Make me sensitive to the warning lights in my heart; keep me from taping over unease or burying it in busyness. If today I must decide on a test report, an expense claim or a promise to a client, remind me to keep my conscience clear before you and before people. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before lunch, ask: what is troubling me today?
Correct one small inaccuracy — a figure or a phrase
Tell a colleague: “I’m not sure about that — I’ll check”
lessons.noon: “Always having a conscience void of offence towards God and men.” — Lord, right now shine on the light that has come on in my heart.

lessons.title: The 321 Five Questions
lessons.theme: Five questions to find God’s way through the grey areas

v: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding.
In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.
But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.

lessons.still: Open the notes app on your phone and write down today’s hardest decision — just one line. Then put the phone down, fold your hands and pray: “Lord, I will not lean on my own understanding. In this matter, please make my path straight.”
teach: Proverbs says, “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” All your ways includes quotations, expense claims, hiring and redundancies — and replying to that difficult email. James adds a promise: whoever lacks wisdom should “ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach”. God will not scold you for asking a “silly question”.

Pilots run through a checklist before every take-off — not because they can’t fly, but because under pressure people miss the critical things. Grey areas need a checklist too. Here are the ‘321 Five Questions’: One, what does Scripture say? Two, what would Jesus do? Three, do I have peace as I pray? Four, does this let Jesus be King, or make me king? Five, who gets the glory — and will this hurt people for the sake of a task?

The five questions are not a vending machine where you insert a dilemma and an answer drops out. They are a framework to slow you down, moving you from relying on yourself with your head to relying on the Spirit with your heart. Sometimes they make the answer crystal clear; sometimes they show you that you need to ask a mature believer, or seek legal or professional advice. Above all, acknowledge him: not asking him to sign off at the last step, but letting him steer from the first.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The three foundations become the first three questions — Scripture is my standard, Jesus is my example, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The last two return to the two cores: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.
lessons.scene: Benjamin works at a financial advisory firm in Singapore. An elderly client trusts him completely and wants to put her entire retirement fund into the product that pays the highest commission. It is legal, but clearly beyond the risk she can bear. His manager hints, “She asked for it. Just process it.” Benjamin looks at the application form, pen hovering over the signature line.
q: Who is God? — He “gives to all liberally and without reproach”. What security does that give you when making decisions?
Who am I? — Which of the five questions do you most often skip?
How shall I respond? — Walk Benjamin through the 321 Five Questions. What should he do?
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane Jesus faced the hardest decision of his life. Falling on his face, he prayed, “Not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39). He was not without feelings; he let the Father’s will be King. Today he walks with you through every crossroads where the choice is hard.
lessons.pray: God of wisdom, I confess that I often lean on my own cleverness, on experience, even on ‘everyone does it’. Before every decision today, remind me to stop and ask: what does Scripture say? What would Jesus do? Give me your peace, and help me choose the path where you are King. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Save the ‘321 Five Questions’ as your lock screen or a note
Run one of today’s decisions through the five questions
Talk through a grey-area problem with a mature believer
lessons.noon: “In all your ways acknowledge him” — Lord, right now, before I decide, I acknowledge you.

lessons.title: Even When It Hurts
lessons.theme: Honesty may cost us, but the upright will never be shaken

v: LORD, who shall dwell in your sanctuary? Who shall live on your holy hill?
He who walks blamelessly and does what is right, and speaks truth in his heart;
he who doesn’t slander with his tongue, nor does evil to his friend, nor casts slurs against his fellow man;
in whose eyes a vile man is despised, but who honours those who fear the LORD; he who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn’t change;
he who doesn’t lend out his money for usury, nor take a bribe against the innocent. He who does these things shall never be shaken.
But even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed. “Don’t fear what they fear, neither be troubled.”

lessons.still: Stand up and plant your feet firmly. Feel the ground holding you for thirty seconds. Pray: “Lord, you are my rock. If honesty costs me today, help me stand firm and not be shaken.”
teach: Psalm 15 opens with a big question: “LORD, who shall dwell in your sanctuary?” The answer is not the person who prays the most eloquently, but the one who “speaks truth in his heart”. One line cuts deep: “he who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn’t change.” The psalmist does not pretend honesty always pays. He admits that telling the truth and keeping your word can leave you out of pocket. But the psalm ends with a promise: “He who does these things shall never be shaken.”

Honesty is like the steel reinforcement in a building. A building that cuts corners looks just as good from outside, and it goes up faster and cheaper — until the earthquake comes. Every time we inflate a quote a little or overpromise a delivery date, we pull one more steel bar out of the pillars of our lives. The cost of honesty is up front; the cost of dishonesty is structural — and it tends to collapse just when you can least afford it.

Peter writes, “Even if you should suffer for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed.” Suffering for doing right is not proof of failure, and failure is not condemnation. We do not earn God’s favour by being honest; because Jesus’ grace has already accepted us, we have the strength to bear honesty’s cost. If refusing to falsify things leads to pressure or threats to your job, alongside a spiritual response please seek out trusted people, or professional help on employment or legal matters, to protect yourself.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Shift your perspective — from the temporary to the eternal. Loss is temporary; character is eternal. Don’t ruin relationships for the sake of things. Letting Jesus receive all the glory sometimes means I receive a little less.
lessons.scene: Jinlong runs a small plumbing and electrical contracting firm in Kuala Lumpur. A big tender is open, and a fellow contractor tells him privately, “Bid low to win it, then make it back on variations.” He knows this would win the job and keep his six workers employed for half a year. The quotation lies on his desk. He picks up his pen.
q: Who is God? — The promise that the upright “shall never be shaken” — what does it show you about God as a keeper?
Who am I? — Have you ever paid a price for honesty? Did it make you trust God more, or fear more?
How shall I respond? — If Jinlong quotes honestly, how might he still care for his workers?
lessons.jesus: Jesus never lied, yet he was condemned for telling the truth. Asked by the high priest whether he was the Christ, he said, “I am” (Mark 14:62) — and was sentenced to death. He paid honesty’s highest price to win our forgiveness, and today he stands with everyone who suffers for doing right.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, you know that honesty sometimes costs me an order or a bonus, or leaves colleagues misunderstanding me. Help me remember that you are my rock. Give me courage to tell the truth and wisdom to tell it gently. When I lose out, please provide for me and remember me yourself. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: In today’s quotes or reports, don’t inflate or hide
Keep one promise you have already made
Pray for a friend who has suffered for being honest
lessons.noon: “He who does these things shall never be shaken.” — Lord, right now I choose to stand on your truth.

mem.t: Do you see a man skilled in his work? He will serve kings. He wont serve obscure men.

lessons.title: Purposed in His Heart
lessons.theme: Inside a foreign system, settle your boundaries in your heart first

v: But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s delicacies, nor with the wine which he drank. Therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.
Now God made Daniel find kindness and compassion in the sight of the prince of the eunuchs.

The prince of the eunuchs said to Daniel, “I fear my lord the king, who has appointed your food and your drink. For why should he see your faces worse looking than the youths who are of your own age? Then you would endanger my head with the king.”
Then Daniel said to the steward whom the prince of the eunuchs had appointed over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah:
“Test your servants, I beg you, ten days; and let them give us vegetables to eat and water to drink.
Then let our faces be examined before you, and the face of the youths who eat of the king’s delicacies; and as you see, deal with your servants.”
So he listened to them in this matter, and tested them for ten days.
At the end of ten days, their faces appeared fairer and they were fatter in flesh than all the youths who ate of the king’s delicacies.
So the steward took away their delicacies and the wine that they were given to drink, and gave them vegetables.

lessons.still: Pick up your first glass of water today and pause before you drink. Pray: “Lord, like Daniel, I settle it in my heart this morning: nothing will defile my relationship with you.” Then drink slowly and hand the day to him.
teach: When Daniel was carried off to Babylon he was still one of the “youths”. The king gave him a new name, a new education and a new diet — a complete programme for turning a young man Babylonian. Daniel accepted the study of the Chaldeans’ language and literature, but he drew a line at the royal table: “Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s delicacies, nor with the wine which he drank.” Scripture doesn’t spell out every reason, but this much is clear: in an environment where others arranged everything for him, he kept one space that belonged to God alone.

His approach is worth studying too. He didn’t overturn the table; he “requested of the prince of the eunuchs”. When he saw the official was afraid for his own head, he proposed a plan to the steward: “Test your servants, I beg you, ten days.” It is like a new employee facing company culture: not confrontation, but a small, measurable, reversible trial. Firm conviction, gentle manner, concrete proposal — Daniel’s workplace toolkit.

Purposing happens in the heart, long before any temptation is put in front of you. Many people decide whether to drink only when they’re already at the client dinner, or whether to take a kickback only when it lands on the desk — and by then it is often too late. Change your thinking and you change your life: set the boundary in prayer first, and you can be gentle yet firm in the moment. And “God made Daniel find kindness and compassion” — God himself opens a way for those who keep their boundaries.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Daniel first guarded his relationship with God in his heart; then he won trust within Babylon’s system, and in time helped build God’s order there.
lessons.scene: Li Na has just been promoted to sales lead at a trading company in Shanghai. Taking her team to dinner with an important client for the first time, her boss hints: “The client loves drinking games. Get him properly drunk tonight and the contract’s ours.” The glasses are filled with baijiu. The client raises his, and the whole table turns to look at her.
q: Who is God? — God made Daniel “find kindness and compassion”. What does that tell you about God’s rule over your workplace?
Who am I? — Is there a boundary at work you have not yet ‘purposed in your heart’?
How shall I respond? — Like Daniel, what proposal could Li Na make that honours the client without crossing the line?
lessons.jesus: After fasting forty days and nights in the wilderness, Jesus was tempted to turn stones into bread. He answered, “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth” (Matthew 4:4). Hungry as he was, he held to his Father’s word — and he has become our strength to overcome in temptation.
lessons.pray: Lord, my workplace can feel like Babylon, with its own food, language and rules. Help me settle it in my heart first, so that nothing defiles my relationship with you. Give me Daniel’s wisdom too — at client dinners, in proposals, in every moment that pushes me to compromise — to keep my boundaries in a gentle and practical way. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down one boundary you are ‘purposing’ to keep
Prepare a gracious way to decline at your next work dinner
Pray for a colleague who is struggling with temptation
lessons.noon: “Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself” — Lord, right now I purpose in my heart to be yours.

lessons.title: Skilled Hands Serve Kings
lessons.theme: Diligence isn’t for climbing; it is work made worthy of the Lord

v: Do you see a man skilled in his work? He will serve kings. He won’t serve obscure men.
The king talked with them; and amongst them all was found no one like Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. Therefore stood they before the king.
In every matter of wisdom and understanding concerning which the king enquired of them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters who were in all his realm.

lessons.still: Look at your hands. Slowly close them into fists and open them again, three times. Pray: “Lord, these hands are your gift. Today make them diligent, precise and willing, doing work worthy of you.”
teach: Proverbs asks, “Do you see a man skilled in his work? He will serve kings.” The Hebrew word carries the sense of being practised and expert — not merely hard-working, but having honed a craft. Daniel and his three friends were like that. They refused the king’s food, but they did not refuse to learn. When the king questioned them, he found them “ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters who were in all his realm”.

Picture an apprentice chopping vegetables in a restaurant kitchen. The head chef won’t start with his CV; he’ll look at his knife work. Is every dice of onion the same size? Is every prep station ready on time? The one who takes care even over chopping onions will one day be called up to the stove. The one who always wants to skip the basics stays at the prep bench forever. Diligence is knife work, day by day, slowly building trust that others can see.

But beware: once diligence becomes ‘proving myself’, it slides into self-centredness — trading performance for approval, filling insecurity with achievement. A Christian’s diligence flows from another source: we are already accepted in Christ, so we can focus on doing the work well without fearing failure. Success is not proof; failure is not condemnation. Standing before kings is a result, not the goal. The real goal is that Jesus receives all the glory.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus is my example — he finished the work his Father gave him. Diligence is not self-centred competition but self-emptied offering: not for my name, but for the Lord’s.
lessons.scene: Yanting is second chef at a Japanese restaurant in Taichung. The head chef keeps giving him the most tedious jobs: sharpening knives, washing rice, sorting the cold store. Others who started with him are already trying new dishes while he’s still prepping. Tonight after closing, he sees a new restaurant offering him more money — and the head chef’s title. His finger hovers over “Apply”.
q: Who is God? — God gave Daniel knowledge and skill in all learning. What does that tell you about how God views our professional abilities?
Who am I? — Is your diligence more about proving yourself, or about serving the Lord?
How shall I respond? — How can Yanting discern whether this is a door God is opening, or his own wish to skip the basics?
lessons.jesus: Before his public ministry, Jesus spent long hidden years in Nazareth. Scripture simply says, “Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and men” (Luke 2:52). He was in no hurry to be seen, yet in the Father’s time he stood before multitudes.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for the abilities and opportunities to learn that you have given me. Rescue me from impatience and comparison. Help me be faithful in the smallest things, making every bit of prep and every email worthy of you. If you are opening a new door, help me see it clearly; if you want me to stay, make me willing. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Spend five extra minutes doing one basic task well
Spend ten minutes learning a new work skill
Thank someone who once taught you your craft
lessons.noon: “Do you see a man skilled in his work? He will serve kings.” — Lord, right now I want only to be diligent before you.

lessons.title: Nothing to Pin on Him
lessons.theme: Work so faithfully that only your faith can be faulted

v: It pleased Darius to set over the kingdom one hundred and twenty local governors, who should be throughout the whole kingdom;
and over them three presidents, of whom Daniel was one, that these local governors might give account to them, and that the king should suffer no loss.
Then this Daniel was distinguished above the presidents and the local governors, because an excellent spirit was in him; and the king thought to set him over the whole realm.

Then the presidents and the local governors sought to find occasion against Daniel as touching the kingdom; but they could find no occasion or fault, because he was faithful. There wasn’t any error or fault found in him.
Then these men said, “We won’t find any occasion against this Daniel, unless we find it against him concerning the law of his God.”

lessons.still: Open today’s calendar and read it from the first item to the last. With each one, quietly say, “Lord, this is yours too.” Let the whole day’s work be placed in his hands before it begins.
teach: By now Daniel had lived in Babylon for decades. Regimes had changed, yet the new king, Darius, still relied on him. His jealous colleagues tried everything to find grounds for charges against him, but “they could find no occasion or fault, because he was faithful. There wasn’t any error or fault found in him.” In the end they had to admit: “We won’t find any occasion against this Daniel, unless we find it against him concerning the law of his God.” What praise — his rivals themselves proved his innocence.

When a company is audited, the real fear is not the inspection but being caught with two sets of books. Daniel’s life had only one set: the same before the king as at home, the same in large matters as in small. His opponents combed through every document and could only attack his faith. If one day someone goes looking for your faults, may the best they can say be: “There’s nothing wrong with this person — except that they take Jesus too seriously.”

This is not perfectionism; it is a transparent life. Daniel had “an excellent spirit”, and his faithfulness flowed from within. The self-centred fear scrutiny, because inside and outside don’t match. The self-emptied are not afraid to be seen, because they have nothing to hide — and if they do get something wrong, they are willing to admit it and correct it. A changed life changes how you live: when your accounts, your timesheets and your promises can all bear inspection, your faith becomes your strongest witness.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change your thinking and you change your life; change your life and you change how you live. The “excellent spirit” within Daniel showed outwardly as “no error or fault”. Only a life changed from the inside out can withstand any audit.
lessons.scene: Yizhen works in the accounts department of a listed company. The new finance director finds her too meticulous and quietly asks someone to ‘dig up something on her’. This week, someone has started going through two years of accounts she handled. A colleague whispers, “Maybe tidy up a few small things first, before they catch you?” She stands at the filing cabinet, her hand on the drawer.
q: Who is God? — Daniel had “an excellent spirit”. Do you believe God can grow that kind of life in you?
Who am I? — If someone went through your work records, which part would you most fear them seeing?
How shall I respond? — Should Yizhen ‘tidy up’ the files, or face the review openly? If she does find a mistake, what should she do?
lessons.jesus: At Jesus’ trial, many false witnesses came forward, yet “they found none” (Matthew 26:60). Pilate too said, “I find no basis for a charge against him” (John 19:6). The sinless one became sin for us, so that we, full of faults, are declared righteous before God.
lessons.pray: Lord who searches hearts, grow an excellent spirit in me, so that my accounts, my hours and my promises can all bear inspection. If someone deliberately looks for my faults, keep my heart from bitterness and panic; if I really have slipped, give me courage to admit it and put it right. May people see only your grace in me. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Check one recent expense claim or timesheet
If you find an error, correct it and tell those affected
Pray one sentence of blessing over someone who makes life hard for you
lessons.noon: “Because he was faithful. There wasn’t any error or fault found in him.” — Lord, right now make me the same inside and out.

lessons.title: Windows Open to Jerusalem
lessons.theme: The greater the pressure, the more we keep our rhythm of meeting God

v: When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room towards Jerusalem) and he knelt on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before.
Then these men assembled together, and found Daniel making petition and supplication before his God.
Evening, morning, and at noon, I will cry out in distress. He will hear my voice.

lessons.still: Put your phone on ‘Do Not Disturb’ for thirty seconds. Turn towards a window or any source of light and pray: “Lord, whatever happens today, the window of my heart is open towards you.”
teach: The decree had been signed: for thirty days, anyone who petitioned any god or man except the king would be thrown into the lions’ den. Daniel knew. He went home, went upstairs to the room whose windows opened towards Jerusalem, and “knelt on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before”. The most moving words are the last: as he did before. This was no emergency prayer meeting called in a crisis; it was a rhythm decades old.

A cardiologist will tell you that a healthy heart depends not on the occasional burst of hard exercise but on a steady rhythm. When pressure comes, rhythm is often the first thing we lose — skipping breakfast, skipping devotions, scrolling until midnight. Daniel’s prayer was the heartbeat of his spiritual life: morning, noon and evening, beating steadily. The psalmist says the same: “Evening, morning, and at noon, I will cry out in distress. He will hear my voice.”

Praying “as he did before” doesn’t mean putting on a show at the office. Daniel prayed in his own house and wasn’t trying to provoke anyone; he simply refused to switch off his relationship with God. You can design your own three windows today: before work, at lunch, on the way home. Rely on the Spirit with your heart; keep your focus on Jesus, not your circumstances. And if long-term overwork is harming your body or mind, talk honestly with your manager, and where needed seek help from trusted people or professionals.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is God → myself → others → tasks. Daniel kept his appointment with God first, and so found strength to face people and pressures. The focus is on Jesus, not on the lions’ den.
lessons.scene: Hannah is a project manager at a marketing agency in Auckland. Since the restructure she has been carrying two teams’ work alone, arriving at seven and leaving at nine. She realises she hasn’t had proper time with God in three weeks. This morning the alarm goes off. She looks at the forty unread emails on her phone, then at the Bible on her bedside table.
q: Who is God? — “He will hear my voice.” What does this God who listens have to do with your pressure?
Who am I? — When pressure comes, what is the first thing you sacrifice?
How shall I respond? — How could Hannah design her ‘three windows’ this morning?
lessons.jesus: As word about Jesus spread and the crowds grew, he “withdrew himself into the desert and prayed” (Luke 5:16). On the night he was betrayed, he went “as his custom was, to the Mount of Olives” (Luke 22:39), and there entrusted himself to the Father. His rhythm has become our refuge under pressure.
lessons.pray: Lord, you know how full my calendar is. Help me, like Daniel, to keep coming to you under pressure, as I always have. This morning, at lunchtime and on the way home, I will keep a window open for you. When the emails pour in, remind me that you will hear my voice. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Set three ‘prayer window’ reminders: morning, noon, evening
Pray for one minute before opening messages at lunch
End today’s work with a worship song on the way home
lessons.noon: “He knelt on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God” — Lord, right now I kneel before you in my heart.

lessons.title: Review: Faithful Stewards
lessons.theme: Reviewing rest, money and integrity with honest correction

v: Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD.
He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.
If therefore you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches?
If you have not been faithful in that which is another’s, who will give you that which is your own?

lessons.still: Find a quiet corner and take three deep breaths. Pray: “Lord, search my work and my life over these past weeks. I’m not here to condemn myself, but to come back to you.”
teach: Lamentations was written after Jerusalem fell. Among the ruins the poet says, “Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD.” We examine ourselves not to sink into gloom but to return. Jesus says, “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.” Through this stage we have been learning to be faithful stewards: giving our time to God in rest, acknowledging that all our money is his, and letting him be King over our integrity.

Many companies carry out an annual stocktake: does what the books say match what is actually on the shelves? A stocktake is not a punishment; it makes next year’s ordering accurate. Our spiritual life needs a stocktake too. Use ‘review and correction’ from the eight steps and ask five questions. Thinking: how do I view time and money? Life: where have I become more like Jesus? Living: does my rest have a rhythm? Relationships: have I hurt anyone over money? Ministry: has my integrity become a witness?

Every stocktake reveals gaps; that is normal. In his parable Jesus speaks of “unrighteous mammon” and “true riches”, reminding us that everything on earth is a temporary trust. When you find a gap, correct one small thing, then practise it again and again. Now open the ‘Workplace Health Self-Check’ in the app and answer honestly. It is not an exam. It lets you and your spiritual companion see together what God has already done in you, and what he wants to do next.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The eight steps — information, revelation, conviction, practice, review, correction, repetition, multiplication. Today we pause at review and correction, so that what this stage has taught becomes real change in our lives, and can be multiplied to others.
lessons.scene: Zhiyuan is a middle manager at a tech company in Hsinchu. Looking back over these months, he started keeping the Lord’s Day as a day of rest, gave part of his bonus first to God, and refused to pad a travel claim. But lately he has been working weekends again, and his giving has stopped for two months. He opens the app and looks at the first question of the ‘Workplace Health Self-Check’, unsure whether to answer honestly.
q: Who is God? — “Turn again to the LORD.” What hope does this God who waits for our return give you as you review?
Who am I? — In rest, money and integrity, what has been your greatest growth, and your biggest gap?
How shall I respond? — Like Zhiyuan, will you complete the ‘Workplace Health Self-Check’ honestly and choose one thing to correct?
lessons.jesus: After his resurrection, Jesus asked Peter by the lakeside, “Do you love me?” (John 21:16) — three times. He was not raking up the past; he was restoring him. Our review, too, takes place under his loving gaze. He sees our gaps, and he himself fills them.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, thank you for leading me these past weeks to learn rest, manage money and keep my integrity. I admit there are places I have grown and places I have slipped back. Shine your light on me, so that I neither condemn myself nor deceive myself. Today I will complete the self-check honestly and correct one small thing. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Complete the ‘Workplace Health Self-Check’ in the app
Write one area of growth each in rest, money and integrity
Choose one gap and set this week’s correction
lessons.noon: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.” — Lord, right now I give you the smallest things.
